author: Anele Mbi
title: Buffalo City’s broken houses and decades of empty promises
content:
A housing rectification project in Braelyn Extension 10 in Buffalo City Municipality (BCM) has left residents frustrated with the municipality’s failure to address severe structural faults.


Serious defects in the RD houses include cracked walls and roofs, leaking roofs, and inadequate foundations. Braelyn residents say they have repeatedly complained to the municipality, which has promised to rebuild the houses since 2004, but has taken no action until today, except for a laydown yard constructed by the sitting, ANC ward councillor, Mendi Wetsetse.


The stalled housing project intersects with service-delivery defects across the ward, including unpaved and potholed roads, poor refuse collection, and electricity shortages brought about by the growing Inkandla informal settlement.


Recently, President Cyril Ramaphosa authorised the Special Investigating Unit (SIU) to probe allegations of extensive corruption and maladministration of major BCM tenders.


According to Braelyn residents, talks about rectifying Braelyn Ext 10 RDP houses began before 2010. The then ward councillor, Thabo Myira, who served as a councillor between 2005 and 2010, confirmed the claim.


Media reports also indicate that in 2009, the then minister of human settlements, Tokyo Sexwale promised people living in faulty RDP houses in East London that their houses would be rebuilt. Today, councillor Wetsetse, who is campaigning for a third term in the upcoming local government election, promised to rectify the situation.


Housing defects


Ntombizanele Mabala, an 80-year-old pensioner, said since residents arrived in Braelyn in 1997, they have complained to councillors and the municipality about the poor condition of their houses, but their pleas were ignored. “These are not houses but hokkies. We have children and a family of six. Rain comes in from every direction – through the roof, the walls and underneath – because these houses have no foundations,” she said. “The councillor promised that the housing rectification process would begin before 4 November, but there are still no signs of work apart from a laydown-yard fence erected two years ago.”


Another pensioner, Nothembile Mqhayi, whose house was built below ground level, said her house floods when it rains. She showed

Elitsha

 a hole she had made at the bottom of a wall to let water that entered the house drain out.


The Mqhayi family had to make a hole in the wall to drain out water when the house floods.


Ziyanda Mpakantsho (42), who recently joined an EPWP project and earns R3,000 a month, said rectification is urgently needed because she lives with a sick and disabled person. “I grew up hearing that the cracks in the walls would be repaired, but many years have passed. These Braelyn houses have no proper foundations, so water leaks in when it rains. The houses have not been rectified because the money is being squandered,” she said.


Zama Thutha (70) said the government had not fixed the RDP houses because it was corrupt and unaccountable to voters. “Even the EPWP jobs created recently will end after the elections. Our system of government is capitalism, which puts profit before the needs of ordinary people,” he said.


Recurring delays and more promises


Responses from both the BCM and the Eastern Cape department of human settlements (DHS) are not only conflicting but also suggest the rectification process remains a false hope for Braelyn residents. When asked whether the municipality or its ward councillor has made any promises of rectification, the municipality said the provincial government is responsible for the rectification process.


“The Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality wishes to clarify that it does not currently run a municipal housing rectification programme; this falls outside local government funding allocations. What we can say is that the laydown yard established on-site remains a site-securing measure for future development once capital is allocated.”


The laydown yard is overgrown

.


The provincial DHS said that, despite the constitutional principle of cooperative governance that compels the various spheres of government to share information and support each other, implementation requires compliance with the necessary technical, administrative, planning, and budgetary processes. The department has not denied the fact that rectification has been recognised for several years.

author: WoMin
title: From Mombasa to Yaoundé, the vision and the demand is for reparative justice
content:
Through WoMin’s work alongside African women organising against extractivism, against the drivers of the climate crisis and its impacts, the destruction of the commons through false solutions, unjust energy transitions (and generally a world order that serves a minority over the global majority), we have been asking: what is the full range of impacts and costs in the face of environmental and climate impacts? Who and whose work absorbs these impacts and costs? And what would repair mean from the perspective of women, their communities and the ecosystems they care for and are cared for at the frontline of the climate crisis, where centuries of continued systems of accumulation by dispossession and destruction meet?


Our experience shows us that reparations cannot simply be another form of compensation. They must confront the very systems producing the harm – extractivism, odious and illegitimate debt, colonial legacies, patriarchy, racism, and corporate power promoting more false solutions whose aim is not climate justice but profit. Reparations must indeed offer us all a real chance to build Pan African feminist futures that centre care, including the restoration of the commons, and the conditions that make life possible.


Connecting the “c-words” – colonialism to climate reparations


The recent

African Symposium on Climate Reparations

 in Mombasa, Kenya, started on that same note: “there is no “c-word” that we cannot bring into conversations on climate reparations”, argued a comrade in his opening remarks. And indeed, the current

climate disorder

1

 is a historical process, and Colonialism (the c-word that in other climate justice spaces some shy away from) is part and parcel of it. As is, we argue at WoMin, capitalism. What is more, not only do climate reparations need to address colonialism and neocolonialism, but also the solution to the climate crisis will not be found within capitalism. Or as Audre Lorde put it, “… the master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house. They may allow us temporarily to beat him at his own game, but they will never enable us to bring about genuine change.”


Not only we need our own tools, but also a broad alliance, as broad, yet united in principles and analysis, as broad and urgent is the task ahead. And the symposium offered an important space to bring together many working for reparations across the continent and in the diaspora, in conversations navigated along four main tracks: rights of nature and ecosystems stewardship; finance, debt and tax justice; law and human rights; and lived realities from frontline communities.


And the timing matters. We are entering the Decade of Justice and Reparations for Africans and People of African Descent, while the debt crisis in Africa continues to exponentially grow and deepen climate vulnerability, false climate solutions continue to expand, further threatening the commons millions of Africans depend upon for their everyday subsistence, and the African Court considers an Advisory Opinion on States’ obligations in the climate crisis.


As powerful expressed in an

open letter

 which emerged from the symposium, a Pan African position and action plan for climate reparations is urgent, but it cannot be constructed only through states, legal and financial tools. Those at the frontlines absorbing the costs of extractivism, ecological destruction and climate disruption have to shape what counts as harm, what constitutes repair, and what must stop. And importantly, we need to organise at all levels the collective power to make repair possible.


African women united for climate justice and reparations


This was the task of the 4th

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA) in Yaoundé, Cameroon, held in early October under the theme, “Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!”. The Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal, and Zambia.


Oh ancestors, watch over Africa and let everything return to Africa! If we are coveted today, if there are wars, it is because our ancestors bequeathed this land to us. They did not abuse its riches. They used them sustainably. So we ask our ancestors to guide us during this Assembly, so that peace and food …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: Adetokunbo Abiola
title: Nigeria’s AI Ambitions vs. The Regulatory Void–Who Protects the Citizens?
content:
Last year, scammers launched a deepfake videos of popular Nigerian social media influencer,

Martins Vincent Otse

, through a fraudulent Facebook campaign. The cybercriminals superimposed a fabricated AI-generated audio on a genuine video of Otse from early 2024.


Martins Vincent Otse


In the cloned voice, Otse introduced an online chatting scheme where viewers could earn up to $1,000 monthly. By cloning the influencer’s face and reputation, the scammers not only harmed Otse’s reputation as a respected influencer, they also preyed on the poverty of many Nigerians, tricking them into becoming a member of an online platform created to appropriate their personal information and savings.


On

October 5

, to show that the issue still mattered, the Nigeria Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) warned organisations and staff against sharing sensitive data with public AI tools.


As the federal government shapes  its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy with the aim to leapfrog development, doctors and nurses use clinical Al tools without standardised verification methods and companies run systems without Al oversight structures. Banks move transactions to automated and Al-driven solutions to combat soaring transaction fraud and manage financial risk, while


87.5 percent

 of  fintech companies now deploy Al for automated fraud detection. In theory, the

Nigeria Data Protection Act

 gave citizens the right to object to automated decision-making; in practice, the abuse of enforcement renders it non-justiceable when Al systems cause harm.


For instance, during the lead up to the 2023 presidential elections, a simulated audio clip went viral, purportedly featuring

former Vice President Abubakar Atiku

 and other members of his party  discussing plans to rig the election. Fact checkers labelled the audio false and generated by artificial intelligence tools. Investigations opened, but there was no prosecution. Defamation laws exist in Nigeria, but none existed to assign blame for the creation of a lie by generative models.


In another instance, unverified screening AIs missed the detection of over

1,247 tuberculosis cases

, as well misclassified

342 high-risk pregnancies

, with

186 preventable patient deaths

 linked to Al diagnostic errors. The tools involved were not registered as medical devices by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control ( NAFDAC), but registered as “wellness” apps.


Driven by the Ministry of Communications and NITDA, the National AI Strategy sets normative ambitions — to align AI deployment with human rights. But with internet penetration now at

68.3 percent penetration

 at

148.2 million

 subscribers, that ambition is no longer aspirational; the state has a functional duty to protect citizens from algorithmic harm at scale.


The issue remains implementation. NITDA has put together a draft

Al Code of Practice

, and the Nigerian Data Protection Commission is enforcing data protection. But broader analytics from NITDA suggest that more than

56 percent

 of government IT projects fail to meet expectations due to procurement, design and implementation flaws. This exposes sensitive consumer data to hackers, increasing the risk of identity theft and digital fraud from design flaws.


In the UK and EU, high-risk AI systems are subject to mandatory pre-deployment conformity assessments. In Nigeria, where banks now use AI-powered tools to identify and prevent fraudulent transactions, no equivalent requirement exists for auditing models against local fraud patterns before they go live.


This institutionalises systemic weaknesses. Angela Olusola was a 46-year-old mother of three. After an unaudited AI flagged her successive transaction as suspicious fraud behaviour, it froze her account. Unfortunately, she lacked financial buffers, with the 48-to-72-hour account freeze meaning she could not buy food, pay her transport fares or restock her business. Since she lived from hand-to-mouth, the algorithm error triggered an immediate poverty crisis.


Algorithmic biases in micro-lending are not abstract. A poor trader who uses a cheap phone and constantly changes SIM cards is flagged as “high risk”. The algorithm sees her behaviour as an indicator of low financial standing or attempts to cheat, resulting in instant loan rejections.


The training data is heavily skewed to salaried, urban, Android users in Lagos.

author: Alicia Houser
title: Tanzania’s peace was never peaceful
content:
One year ago, on October 29, 2025, the sound of bombs and bullets rang out around Dar es Salaam and several other cities across Tanzania. Before last year’s election, Tanzania had enjoyed an international reputation as a peaceful haven in an often tumultuous region. Foreign governments and tour companies certainly helped craft this image, but so did Tanzania’s government and population. Since I started visiting the country in 2017, people have often cited

amani

 (peace) as one of Tanzania’s best attributes. People attributed this purported peace not to satisfaction with the government or living conditions, but to fear.

Watanzania ni woga

 (Tanzanians are cowards), my friends tell me self-deprecatingly. This fear belies the peaceful image Tanzania has cultivated overseas. 

Histories, or perhaps more accurately colonial histories, place Tanzania in the category of African countries that peacefully acquired independence. To consider Tanzania’s transition to independence as peaceful is to take a short view of history. This narrative ignores the Hehe killed during seven years of fighting against the Germans, which ended in 1898 with

Chief Mkwawa

 killing himself rather than surrendering and his skull being taken to Germany. It ignores the organized resistance that involved the entire southern half of Tanzania, the

Maji Maji

 war of 1905–1908, which some consider the first Pan-African anticolonial resistance movement. The Tanzanian historian Gilbert Gwassa estimated that 300,000 Africans died in this movement, most of them from starvation. The narrative of peaceful transition also ignores the roughly 600,000 Africans who died as a result of

World War I

 military incursions on Tanzanian soil. In these three events alone, almost one million would-be Tanzanians lost their lives to colonization. 

I was in Dar es Salaam last year during the election. The internet cut out at about noon, and the sounds of bombs and bullets started around 1pm and continued off and on for another four days. Without internet, radio, or television, I got my news the old-fashioned way: through other people. My friends in Arusha and Moshi sent frequent messages, and I went out to my courtyard and sat with my neighbors who were connected to other cities across the country. We exchanged what we had heard: someone’s niece had stepped outside her apartment in Dar and encountered a body, Muhimbili Hospital was overflowing, bodies were being stacked outside mortuaries, ballot boxes had been burned. There would be no votes to count. By day three of the lockdown, rumors were circulating that the government was preparing for a prolonged battle, and that Dar’s drinking water might be poisoned. By day five, the store next door to me had sold out of airtime, water, sodas, and milk. Amid the fear, though, was excitement.

Watanzania wameamka,

 one of my neighbors said proudly. Tanzanians have woken up. A neighbor who stopped by noted that

hakuna mafanikio bila

 sacrifice. No success without sacrifice. Another neighbor said she was going to give 10,000 shillings to any

bodaboda

 and

bajaji

 drivers (the motorcycle and three-wheeler taxi drivers who ferry much of urban Tanzania) she saw; they were the ones leading the protests.

On day six, Mama Samia — as President Samia Suluhu Hassan is popularly known — was sworn in as president at a ceremony closed to the public. The sounds of bombs and bullets had fizzled out over the days, and the morning marking one week since the election radiated with the usual city sounds of buses,

bajajis

, and

bodabodas

 that had gone quiet for so long. The halt in violence did not result from any recognition by Samia of the illegitimacy of the election, which did not include any candidates from the country’s main opposition parties. The electoral commission barred Chadema, the largest of them, and disqualified the candidate of ACT-Wazalendo. After days of police shooting

live rounds

 into crowds and indiscriminately killing

civilians

 caught in the wrong place at the wrong time, the protests stopped. Tanzanians decided they did not want to die. After the election, there was a general feeling of “Where do we go from here?”.

Months before the election, in March of last year, I attended a memorial event on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in Old Moshi, remembering the 19 area chiefs whom the Germans hanged on March 2, 1900, on accusations of subversion. One of the elders recalled a phrase he heard often growing …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Feds declare Roberts Bank 2 expansion ‘project of national interest’
content:
A large-scale port expansion to be located off the coast of Delta, B.C., has been labelled as a ‘project of national interest,’ a designation which, according to environmental advocates, could result in the extinction of the Southern Resident Killer Whales.

In an email sent to APTN News on the heels of the announcement, Julia Levin, the associate director of national climate at Environmental Defence, wrote that not only is this “bad news for orcas,” but that it may be “a run-around on the Species at Risk Act, given that was the only approval that the project didn’t have.”

Robert Banks Terminal 2 is an expansion of the Port of Vancouver, operated by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority (VFPA) and located on 130 hectares (about 200 soccer pitches) of marine land off the B.C. coast.

According to a release from Ottawa, the project would add 2.4 million containers of annual capacity, increasing it by “approximately 50 per cent.”

It would also support “up to $100 billion in annual trade,” therefore “helping Canada achieve its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2035.”

It meets the criteria of what can be considered a project in the national interest, according to Bill C-5, the Building Canada Act, which are that it must “strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security”; “provide economic or other benefits”; “advance the interests of Indigenous Peoples”; and “contribute to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s climate change objectives.”

Once this criteria is met, major projects may be exempt from certain laws, such as the Species at Risk Act.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that, “By listing Roberts Bank Terminal 2 as a project of national interest, we are better connecting our economy with the world and diversifying our trade. As the world competes for capital, Canada will not wait. We are building a stronger, more independent, and more competitive Canadian economy.”

However, the project is also slated to be built in the Fraser River Estuary, which has already lost more than 85 per cent of floodplain habitat and supports 102 species at risk, according to Levin.

“The estuary is critical habitat for salmon and SRKW, southern resident killer whales, as confirmed by DFO and the environmental assessment of the project – which assessed that the new terminal would result in destruction of the legally protected Southern Resident Killer Whale’s critical habitat,” she wrote.

A 2020 environmental assessment for the project determined that it would cause “significant adverse environmental effects” on Chinook salmon, wetlands, and the resident whales, which have been listed as critically endangered since 2003.

An application for a Species at Risk permit, which would allow the building of the Roberts Bank 2 port in the habitat, was filed on Oct. 28, 2024, with a deadline of Oct. 28, 2026 — two days ago, as of publishing.

‘An incredible animal’: B.C. port expansion could drive southern resident killer whales to extinction, advocates warn

As of Friday morning, the tool used to track the permit’s progress on Canada’s website indicated it was overdue, but by the afternoon, the page had been wiped.

Canada held a consultation period while it considered the national interest designation, which began

In a letter sent to the Major Projects Office by Raincoast Conservation Foundation, the advocacy and research organization wrote that “Designation as a PONI is not an appropriate use of the Building Canada Act.

“Raincoast is concerned that the national interest cannot be reduced to container capacity, trade volume and construction speed when the proposal is in the Fraser River Estuary. Promises and investments announced by the federal government … to ensure prosperity by combining regulatory certainty with environmental protection are an insufficient guarantee given the level of harm identified from this project.”

Levin stated that, “by declaring this mega-port as a ‘project of national interest,’ Prime Minister Carney has dealt a devastating blow to the last remaining Southern Resident Killer Whales.

“This political moment will pass, but extinction is forever.”

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Family searches for missing Inuk teen in Ottawa
content:
The mother of a missing 14-year-old Inuk girl is hoping her daughter will find her way home as Ottawa police and community members continue searching for her.


“I just want her home,” Julian Oyukuluk said in an interview Friday about her daughter, Lydia.


Lydia Oyukuluk was last seen Wednesday, Oct. 28, between 5:45 and 6 p.m. in the 1000 block of Gladstone Avenue, where she lives with her family, her mother said. It’s a bit south of the Hintonburg neighbourhood and a few blocks west of Preston Street’s Little Italy area.


Julian said she expected Lydia to return home that night. Lydia left without her cellphone, which is now with investigators, her mother said.


Family members, friends and members of Ottawa’s Inuit community have joined the search, Julian said. So far, they have looked in Major’s Hill Park near the Parliament Buildings and along the Rideau Canal.


“She’s very easy to approach,” Julian said of her daughter. “She’s friendly and she’s sensitive.”


The family is originally from Arctic Bay and has lived in Ottawa for more than a year, Julian said.


On Friday, Ottawa police asked residents in the 1000 block of Gladstone Avenue, including along Spadina Avenue and surrounding streets, to check their backyards, sheds, garages and other places where Lydia might have sought shelter.


Police are also asking residents to review doorbell camera and surveillance footage from Wednesday evening onward for possible sightings.


And police released a second picture of Lydia in which she’s wearing a prominent cross necklace. But police weren’t able to say whether she was wearing it when she went missing.


Lydia is described as four-foot-nine with a petite build and long black hair partially dyed red at the back.


She was last seen wearing baggy black sweatpants, a black camouflage hoodie and socks. She was not wearing shoes.


Ottawa police have also released an additional photo of Lydia taken before she went missing. The image is the most recent one available to police showing her appearance and build, said Ottawa Police media spokesperson Const.

Fern

 John-Simon.


Anyone who sees Lydia Oyukuluk is asked to call 911 so she can receive immediate assistance, an updated release said. Anyone with information about her whereabouts can contact Ottawa police at 613-236-1222.

title: In the Crosshairs of the Far-Right Advance : An Update on Anti-Fascists and Anarchists in Greece

Anarchist graffiti from Athens, Greece (2026)


The anarchist movement in Greece faces a new wave of repression. Urged on by the US and its obsession with combatting “far-left extremism,” the Greek state has targeted anti-authoritarians with new legal charges and attacked demonstrations, while fascists carry out street attacks and plot their return to the halls of power. Amidst a landscape of ongoing austerity, terrorism designations, lethal prisons, and ferocious wildfires, anarchists nonetheless continue to forge a combative culture of revolutionary solidarity.


In this article, we present an interview with an anarchist comrade in Athens assessing the current situation among anarchists and anti-fascists in Greece, along with analysis of the US’s role in advancing state repression and fantasies of Western supremacy.


The US and Greece: A Right-Wing Alliance to Defend “The West”

With the historic Acropolis and the Parthenon—that ancient symbol of Western democracy, constructed with slave labor—in the background, he delivered a warning message to Greece’s political and business elite.


“The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” Rubio cautioned. “We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.” Lamenting how “nationalism became a dirty word,” he called for renewed militarism, praised Christian faith and martyrdom, and announced a new counterterrorism information-sharing program between the two countries. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio constructs an elaborate photo op for his defense of nationalism, militarism, and “the West” (October 7, 2026).

Greece’s right-wing politicians and business leaders benefiting from the country’s endless austerity measures are heeding Rubio’s call to preserve the hubris of the so-called West. Meanwhile, governments are collaborating to escalate repression against any truly revolutionary movements that challenge the world’s current status quo.


Greece’s strategic importance to Western powers is rooted in its symbolic status as the birthplace of “Western Civilization,” as well as its strategic location in the world today. More recently, the Greek people were pummeled by the 2008 global economic crisis, brought on in part by Wall Street firms such as Goldman Sachs that raked in immense profits while destabilizing the world’s economy and immiserating millions. The US then contributed to the austerity measures imposed on Greece in 2010 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), leading to years of ferocious resistance to neoliberal capitalism and government complicity.


Today, Greece’s current New Democracy regime upholds

the legacy of the brutal military junta

 of 1967-1974, promoting the image of Greece as a symbol European supremacy as invoked by Rubio. Despite its nationalist rhetoric, the government continues to lick the boots of the US, crushing opposition in the streets and enforcing a never-ending precarity on the majority of Greece’s increasingly exhausted and numb population.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: While Americans Paid $148B Extra on Gas Amid War, Big Oil Made $130B in Profits
content:
“All the excess cash we’re accumulating will ultimately be directed toward our owners,” one oil executive bragged.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

As Americans have been forced to shell out an extra $148 billion on gas and diesel in eight months of war on Iran, Big Oil has reaped record profits — with U.S. companies having made over $130 billion in profits, a new analysis finds.

According to The New York Times, these profits were spread across 50 large U.S. oil and gas companies. Many of these companies, like Valero Energy, reported their highest-ever quarterly profits in recent months.

The calculation of oil and gas companies’ collective profits between April and September is conservative, the Times notes, and doesn’t include two months of the war.

Even still, $130 billion is nearly three times more than the industry’s profits this time last year. ExxonMobil more than doubled and Chevron nearly tripled profits in Q3 compared to 2025, and both companies are forecasted to potentially make record profits for the full year.

Meanwhile, prices for consumers have not just hit record highs amid the war, but have also sustained an average price above $4 a gallon for a record amount of time.

According to a tracker set up by Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab, Americans have paid an extra $147 billion on gas and diesel since the start of the war, amounting to over $1,100 per household. Moody’s Analytics has estimated that, when higher prices for jet fuel are accounted for, the war has cost U.S. households $1,184 more just on these fuel prices alone.

These extra costs compound upon an existing affordability crisis across the country, lining the pockets of oil and gas executives as Americans struggle to afford basic necessities like housing and groceries.

“Over time, all the excess cash we’re accumulating will ultimately be directed toward our owners,” Valero Energy’s chief financial officer Homer Bhullar said in a call with Wall Street analysts last week.

Polling by Gallup finds that the war on Iran and gas prices rank as one of the top issues for voters this midterm election season, following the economy as the top concern.

Despite this, President Donald Trump has not just downplayed the war’s impacts on U.S. households, but has openly bragged about the oil and gas industry’s profits spurred by his aggression. “Because of the price of oil, Texas and Oklahoma and North Dakota and all these places, we’re making a fortune,” Trump said at a rally in Arizona this month.

“I can just see the fake headlines: ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn. I’m gonna say it. We’re making a freaking fortune,’” Trump told a crowd in Georgia last weekend.

Several states with Republican-controlled legislatures have implemented temporary gas tax holidays ahead of the midterm elections, hoping to take heat off GOP candidates. However, the measures are just a band-aid on a much larger problem: a war that the Trump administration seems desperate to end, but that they only know how to prolong.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

author: Madelyn Amos
title: ¡Sí Se Puede!: Dolores Huerta’s Feminist Legacy Lives On
content:
Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader, civil rights activist, and feminist who devoted her life to advancing equality and justice, has died at the age of 96. Her groundbreaking work reshaped the labor and feminist movements, leaving an enduring legacy of grassroots organizing, women’s leadership, and collective action that continues to inspire generations.

Huerta was a dear friend and ally of the Feminist Majority Foundation since its founding. She served on the organization’s board for more than 30 years, offering her passion, energy, and visionary leadership to the fight for gender equality.

In the 1980s, Feminist Majority co-founders Eleanor Smeal and Kathy Spillar recruited Huerta to join the Feminization of Power campaign to increase women’s representation in elected office. For four years, Huerta traveled across the country with the Feminist Majority. She mentored women running for office, particularly Latinas and other women of color, and helped them secure endorsements while campaigning alongside them.

Reflecting on their work together, Smeal recalled, “We traveled to 8 states and she was determined to change the composition of California’s state legislature — and she did. When we started the campaign in 1987, the state legislature was only 14.2% women, but because of Dolores, it quickly jumped to 24.2%. And today, the California legislature is 49.2% women.” Now, in Congress, women are 42% of congressional Democrats, getting closer and closer to parity every year.

Spillar added in her memories of the tour with Huerta, “We would gather women active in their communities in their living rooms and talk about the need for more women to run for office. Dolores would always say to them ‘if you can’t recruit someone, then one of you has to step forward and run.’”

Huerta’s tireless organizing helped build momentum for a historic increase in women’s political representation, culminating in the 1992 election widely known as the “Year of the Woman.”

Smeal continued, “She would just keep going, it didn’t matter if it was midnight or 2am. She was my kind of person and we would just stay up all night strategizing. She worked day in and day out for women’s rights, labor rights, civil rights, LGBTQ rights, environmentalism — she was a leader in all the key issues. Her passion was infectious and inspiring.”

Smeal remembers a conversation with Huerta about the lasting impact of their activism. Huerta told her, “Our daughters can have a very different life than us because of the work we did.” Her work will live on in the movements she helped build and the generations who will carry her legacy forward.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Manitoba, community protests legislation that would fast-track resource projects: ‘Have we not lost enough?’
content:
About 100 people attended a demonstration outside the Manitoba legislature on Saturday, ahead of Monday’s First Nations – First Ministers’ meeting where Bill C-39 was on the agenda in Ottawa. Photo by Crystal Greene


Indigenous people in Manitoba are protesting against proposed federal legislation that aims to fast-track resource development — saying it undermines their rights and sovereignty over their lands.


Activists point to several pieces of legislation that they worry would cause more harm to their territories, which are already impacted by climate change and the biodiversity crisis. They also have safety concerns over “man camps” created by industry and potential harms to vulnerable Indigenous women and girls.


Both

Bill C-5

 and

Bill C-39

 are set to fast-track major infrastructure projects in “Canada,” by designating them to be of “national interest.” C-5 was passed in 2025, and C-39 is in its third reading. Meanwhile, the proposed

Bill C-37

 — under review after a second reading — has heightened concerns over First Nations water rights. 


One such

project of “national interest”

 is

Churchill Plus

. It would see a pipeline and terminal built to internationally export LNG through the Port of Churchill on Hudson Bay. The arctic deepwater seaport would also handle increased mining exports out of Manitoba, eventually including the

Ring of Fire

.


About 20 people gathered outside of the Manitoba Legislature on Monday rallying against the legislation and in response to the First Nations-first ministers meeting in Ottawa, which was part of similar solidarity events that happened across “Canada.”


It was one of a few protests in Manitoba in late October against the bills and the extractive projects being pushed through by colonial governments despite opposition. 


People who once stood together in the same spot – the Manitoba legislature – during Idle No More, are standing together again to oppose the fast tracking of major infrastructure projects. Photo by Crystal Greene


Alex Wilson

 of Opaskwayak Cree Nation, a professor in the Faculty of Education at the University of Winnipeg, and an organizer with Idle No More, was at Monday’s rally outside the legislature


Wilson read

a collective statement from Idle No More

 founders that said “the conditions that gave rise to Idle No More in 2012 are confronting us again.”


Wilson said that includes “sweeping legislative changes, threats to environmental protections, and government decisions affecting Indigenous territories without respecting the authority of the people who belong to those lands.”


Wilson told IndigiNews that there’s been “a constant erosion of treaty rights of Indigenous sovereignty and legislation that protects land, water and the sky.”


“The bills that are proposed are kind of galvanising our understanding that this is an agenda that is continually harming First Nations, Indigenous peoples and our environment.”


At another earlier rally at the Manitoba legislature, on Saturday, Indigenous activists and allies spoke against Bills C-39 and C-37.  It was a finale of the

Arctic Crossroads Tour

 in Manitoba that visited Churchill, Nisichawayasihk, Thompson, Brandon, and Winnipeg.


Anishinaabe water protector Taylor Galvin who works closely with Manitoba First Nations that are impacted by hydro projects on their lands, attended the event.


Taylor Galvin spoke during Saturday’s event to oppose Bills C-37 and C-39 outside the Manitoba legislature. Photo by Crystal Greene


“Have we not lost enough? We are living in a ticket time bomb, and our lands and our waters don’t have time, and in Manitoba, our sturgeon relatives don’t have time,” said Galvin, who is from Baaskaandibewi-ziibiing (Brokenhead Ojibway Nation).


“Our fish and our waters are already sick, traces of life-threatening metals like mercury, lead, arsenic, and cadmium are being found in those fish and in those waters.”


Galvin spoke of political greed and “a broken system” that has harmed the environment and continues to extract from it.


“We have a broken system and yet they want more, Bill C-39, removing Indigenous rights, and trying to move forward at a very quick pace for projects of ‘national interest,’” Galvin said.


“Why aren’t the people considered national interests? What aren’t the animals considered national interests? Why are they talking about these things without protecting anything?”

title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Trailer Has Sapphic Sex and Sad Exes
content:
Season one of The Hunting Wives was a wild ride, and I have a feeling season two is going to be even wilder. The full trailer dropped and it has me clapping and kicking my feet at the sapphic chaos about to descend upon us.

The trailer opens with Sophie’s husband asking if Sophie is “still dreaming about her” (“her” being Margo) and a few flashing scenes implies that yes, yes she is.

Other things we see flash by: a glam cowgirl photo shoot, Margo being manipulative to all kinds of people, and Callie being a sad ex and using a photo of Margo as target practice.

This show also knows exactly what it is and is leaning into it. For example, the song playing is Nancy Sinatra’s “Bang Bang”, which is the perfect backdrop for this trailer full of guns and sex and chaos. And the tagline for the season is “someone is going down,” which the narrator says while the visuals cut between a dead body and also a more…explicit interpretation of the phrase.

Based on how season one ended, I can’t wait to find out how Sophie ends up back in Margo’s bed (and her bubble bath!), and luckily we only have one month left to wait.

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. Immigration restrictions present an analogous case: they …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Family of Miranda Mamakwa seeking criminal investigation into ‘negligent’ death of mother
content:
The family of a woman who died after a federal program did not arrange transportation to medical appointments is asking for a criminal investigation.

“The criminal justice system should only be invoked where grounds exist to believe a crime has been committed,” read the statement from the family. “Public officials are as accountable as anyone else in this country for reckless acts that endanger those in their charge.”

According to her family, Miranda Mamakwa died on Sept. 8 after she didn’t receive transportation to multiple important appointments following an open-heart surgery.

She was 31 and the mother of three kids.

“Literally, the blood of Indigenous people is required for any kind of meaningful change,” said Julian Falconer, legal counsel for the family. “We have created a pattern of behavior where we only get their attention once they [Canada] have killed somebody.”

Mamakwa was a member of Fort Severn First Nation, the northernmost community in Ontario, and was relying on transportation from the Non-Insured Health Benefits Program (NIHB) to get to follow-up appointments in Thunder Bay after her surgery in April 2026.

NIHB is a federal program provided by Indigenous Services Canada (ISC), and is mandated to provide medical transportation services, alongside other supports such as medication and vision care, to First Nations and Inuit people.

Her first appointment following her return home was scheduled for May 28, and the local nursing station had sent a request by fax (the only method of communication with NIHB offices available to them, Falconer confirmed) for NIHB to provide transportation.

However, the nearest office, located in Sioux Lookout, never got back to them.

Despite multiple requests and letters from her doctor, she missed four appointments, including “an appointment with a vascular surgeon about blood clots,” according to the backgrounder provided to the media.

The backgrounder also stated that, following the surgery, Mamakwa had been put on blood thinner medication for blood clots, and was visiting the Nation’s nursing station once a week for blood work.

She eventually became lethargic and “began to lose feeling in her fingers,” the backgrounder noted, and she ultimately died of a brain haemorrhage after being transported to Thunder Bay.

Brain haemorrhages are caused by a blood vessel leaking or bursting in the brain, essentially drowning it.

Prior to her death, on Aug. 19, Mamakwa had made a grim post on social media: “If I die, please go after them.”

On Friday, Falconer and Mamakwa’s parents, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, issued a statement announcing they had sent a formal request to Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner Thomas Carrique.

“The wanton and reckless disregard shown for Miranda’s health, and ultimately her life, by those public officials responsible for arranging her medical transportation makes such an investigation a necessity,” the statement said.

Eva and Mike are staying out of the public eye, but did comment in the statement.

“This should never have happened to Miranda. She should be alive today,” they said. “We deserve to know how something like this happened, and we want the individual or individuals responsible for failing to respond to these urgent requests for transportation to be held accountable. They cost Miranda her life. They cost her children a future without their mother.”

Mother of First Nations woman who couldn’t get medical transport and died seeks reform

Falconer said he does not take criminal cases lightly, but that this circumstance was “wonton neglect.”

“Three children are without a mother. A grandmother is left explaining to these children where their mother is. Words cannot describe the extent of the neglect here,” he said.

It’s also indicative of Canada’s failure to act in the best interests of Indigenous Peoples, he said.

Alongside this matter, the lawyer is also legal counsel to a coalition of several First Nations and tribal councils, led by Wunnumin Lake First Nation, Matawa Chiefs Council, and Windigo First Nations Council, which filed a human rights complaint against ISC on Oct. 1.

“The complaint alleges widespread neglect and systemic discrimination by the NIHB, whose routine administrative failures effectively deny life-sustaining healthcare to remote, fly-in communities,” stated a release on the Falconers legal practice’s website.

The coalition is seeking “sweeping structural overhauls,” as well as $20,000 in damages …

author: Solange Guimarães
title: Fuga de Flávio abre caminho para bolsonarismo abraçar políticos para além do sobrenome
content:
A derrota de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) para Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) nas eleições presidenciais e sua fuga para os Estados Unidos abriram uma disputa pela liderança da extrema direita brasileira que pode resultar em um bolsonarismo cada vez menos dependente dos membros da família do ex-presidente.


Para três pesquisadores que estudam a extrema direita, ouvidos pela

Agência Pública

, o episódio pode representar o início de uma mudança mais profunda: a separação entre o capital político acumulado pelo bolsonarismo na última década e a família que deu nome ao movimento. A crise dos herdeiros de Jair Bolsonaro, entretanto, não significa necessariamente uma perda de influência da extrema direita, que poderá manter sua agenda política, sua capacidade de mobilização e sua atuação nas instituições mesmo sob novas lideranças.


Michelle Bolsonaro, o governador reeleito de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), e o deputado federal Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) estão entre os nomes citados pelos acadêmicos que podem ganhar espaço na reorganização do movimento, que perdeu a disputa pelo Palácio do Planalto, mas ampliou sua presença no Congresso Nacional.


“Acho que todo mundo, de uma certa forma, respira aliviado com a fuga do Flávio. Porque isso significa que há espaço dentro do bolsonarismo para além da família Bolsonaro”, afirma a antropóloga Isabela Kalil, pesquisadora especializada na extrema direita brasileira. Segundo ela, o senador não dispõe de capital político próprio suficiente para exercer, a partir do exterior, a liderança que seu pai construiu no país.


Pesquisadora da extrema direita no Brasil, Isabela Kalil enxergar espaço no bolsonarismo sem os Bolsonaros


A avaliação é compartilhada pelo filósofo Rodrigo Nunes, professor da PUC-Rio e professor visitante da University of Essex, no Reino Unido. Para ele, a disputa pela sucessão já alcança o interior da própria família. “Parece que a briga pela sucessão está se abrindo dentro da própria família Bolsonaro, porque todo mundo percebe que o grande nome dentro da família agora é claramente a Michelle.”


A historiadora e cientista política Tatiana Vargas-Maia, professora de Relações Internacionais da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), aponta uma transformação ainda mais ampla. “Talvez a gente veja a morte do bolsonarismo como identidade, mas uma manutenção dele como estratégia”, afirma. Na avaliação da pesquisadora, o movimento pode abandonar gradualmente a dependência da figura de Jair Bolsonaro sem abrir mão das práticas políticas, eleitorais e de mobilização desenvolvidas nos últimos dez anos.


A reorganização foi necessária após a vitória do presidente Lula no segundo turno, com 51,79% dos votos válidos, contra 48,21% de Flávio Bolsonaro. O senador recebeu quase 60 milhões de votos, mas deixou o país dois dias depois, apesar de uma determinação do ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Alexandre de Moraes, para que entregasse seus passaportes à Polícia Federal.


Flávio chegou a Miami na quarta-feira (28), acompanhado da mulher e das duas filhas, após passar pela Argentina onde pegou um vôo particular com escala no Equador. Já nos Estados Unidos, divulgou uma carta em que se apresentou inicialmente como o verdadeiro presidente do Brasil, apesar da derrota nas urnas. Posteriormente, alterou o documento para se autodeclarar líder do país, mantendo acusações de fraude eleitoral sem apresentar provas.


Entre aliados, as decisões de Flávio provocaram reações que evidenciaram o seu isolamento. desde Tarcísio de Freitas defendeu o reconhecimento do resultado das urnas, enquanto Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), coordenador da campanha presidencial do PL, afirmou que não havia elementos para sustentar as acusações de fraude. O distanciamento reforça as dificuldades de Flávio para se apresentar como líder da oposição a partir do exterior.


Michelle e Tarcísio despontam na disputa pela sucessão


Como senadora, Michelle Bolsonaro pode consolidar a sua liderança no bolsonarismo


Lideranças do campo conversador não demoraram a enxergar o espaço construído pela fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro. Para os pesquisadores, Michelle Bolsonaro e Tarcísio de Freitas são os nomes com maior destaque nessa reorganização até o momento, embora a disputa também envolva políticos mais jovens e movimentos que não se identificam integralmente com o bolsonarismo.


Rodrigo Nunes considera improvável que os filhos 01 e 03 de Jair Bolsonaro, dos Estados Unidos, consigam manter …

author: Nahuel Lag
title: El suelo como espejo de la relación entre humanidad y naturaleza
content:
Por Patricia Fernández y Lourdes Gil Cardeza*


Somos muchas las personas, organizaciones e instituciones que reconocemos estar atravesando una crisis civilizatoria muy profunda. Hay tantísima evidencia que muestra cómo estamos sobrepasando los límites físicos que permiten nuestra existencia en el planeta Tierra. Hay un área específica de la economía que lo estudia: la economía ecológica. El estilo de vida que impone la sociedad occidental implica calentamiento global, una creciente y continua contaminación de suelos y aguas, y el constante despojo de tierras a pueblos indígenas y campesinos debido al avance del modelo económico, que pone en jaque a los procesos biológicos de la vida que han ido coevolucionando desde hace, al menos, 460 millones de años, cuando empezó a desarrollarse la vida fuera del agua.


El suelo es un espejo de los vínculos que lo conforman. Es la resultante de la convivencia evolutiva entre la roca madre, el clima y los seres vivos. En otras palabras, el suelo es parte de los procesos del planeta Tierra, el suelo es vida, el suelo está vivo. Tanto su color oscuro característico como ese olorcito que percibimos corresponden a la materia orgánica (componente fértil y vital del suelo), compuesta por los organismos vivos que lo habitan y por lo muerto en vía de descomposición que nutren de manera espiralada a los organismos y las plantas de las que nos alimentamos. El estilo de vida occidental pone en riesgo esa vitalidad.


El tipo de agricultura que domina al planeta no es un simple conjunto de técnicas para producir alimentos (y muchas veces commodities): es la materialización de una lógica de poder que entrelaza colonialismo, patriarcado y capitalismo. Así lo evidencian las voces críticas de pensadoras que ayer y hoy señalan cómo el avance sobre la tierra y la naturaleza es un reflejo de la misma lógica de dominación ejercida sobre los cuerpos de las mujeres y los territorios. Llegar a comprender la crisis o la degradación del suelo hoy, exige, en principio, desentrañar esta trama histórica y epistemológica que ha convertido a la naturaleza en un objeto de explotación ilimitada. 


Creemos que hacer el intento por desarmar esta trama (o trampa), es condición necesaria en el proceso de deconstrucción que elegimos, como dijo

Audre Lorde

, para transformar la ira en un proceso creativo. Con este texto buscamos traer a la actualidad, y a latinoamérica en particular, a Eve Balfour, una mujer de la aristocracia inglesa quien, con mucha claridad y simpleza, se atrevió a abordar temas invisibilizados en Europa y sus continentes colonizados, al publicar su libro

El Suelo Vivo

 (

The Living Soil

) en 1943. 


Foto: Matías sarlo - Minga


Esta tesis describe de manera sencilla los vínculos entre la salud humana y el cultivo de nuestros alimentos y pone la lupa en el suelo jerarquizando su rol como promotor de la salud toda. En palabras de Eve:

“La evidencia acumulada sobre la interrelación entre la vitalidad del suelo y la salud de las plantas, los animales y el ser humano es de tal importancia y de tan profundas implicancias que ya es hora de que el público en general tenga la oportunidad de estudiar y formarse su propio juicio al respecto”

.


La matriz del despojo


La crítica al modelo agrícola industrial debe partir de la constatación de que su origen no es meramente técnico, sino profundamente político. La antropóloga maya-kaqchikel

Aura Cumes

 sostiene que el patriarcado colonial llega desde Europa y se reconfigura en América para ejercer el sometimiento sobre las mujeres, las poblaciones indígenas y afrodescendientes convirtiéndolas en sujetos despojables y así validar la extracción del territorio y del cuerpo-territorio. Este proceso de dominación tuvo un pilar fundamental: la disociación del hombre respecto de la naturaleza, a la cual se feminizó para legitimar su conquista. "A partir de ello —explica Cumes— se atribuye la potestad de descubrirla, penetrarla, torturarla y convertirla en mercancía." 


Esta visión no es casual, sino que se fundamenta tanto en los textos bíblicos que otorgan al hombre el "señorío" sobre la creación como en el discurso científico que adoptó estos postulados como base de su conocimiento. En esta trama (o trampa), el capitalismo manifiesta la continuidad de las mismas lógicas que motorizaron al colonialismo al implementar la sustitución de ecosistemas enteros por una "biota mixta" europea (trigo, ganado vacuno, cerdos, malezas, microorganismos, personas) …

title: ATE protestó frente al Ministerio de Defensa por el cierre de la IOSFA
content:
La movilización rechazó la decisión del Gobierno nacional de ‘disolver y liquidar’ el funcionamiento de la Obra Social de las Fuerzas Armadas (ex IOSFA) y que afecta a 352.000 afiliadas y afiliados a nivel nacional.


Fotos: Camila Rey y Chiqui Rodríguez.


Este jueves ATE llevó adelante una Jornada Nacional de Protesta en defensa de las funciones de la Obra Social de las Fuerzas Armadas y del Personal Civil (IOSFA/OSFA), ante la reciente resolución impuesta por el Gobierno nacional que disuelve y liquida el organismo, poniendo en riesgo la continuidad laboral de 1450 trabajadoras y trabajadores.

Mercedes Cabezas, Secretaria General Adjunta de ATE Nacional, expresó: “Multitudinaria la marcha que protagonizamos al Ministerio de Defensa, en defensa del trabajo de 1450 trabajadoras y trabajadores, de las farmacias y de los hoteles de la antigua IOSFA, actual OSFA. También para construir una política de defensa y de seguridad que tenga en cuenta los deseos, las necesidades y los derechos del pueblo argentino. El genocidio planificado de Javier Milei que ataca el sistema de salud, de defensa, de seguridad, y lo pone al servicio de políticas colonizadoras, genera no solo que se vacíe la obra social sino que se atente contra nuestro pueblo porque el sistema de salud está desfinanciado. Esta obra social, que es la única nacional estatal que queda en pie en la Argentina, es entregada a manos privadas, a Medicus que fue la primera prepaga que se acercó a hacerse cargo de la Prefectura y Gendarmería y comenzó el vaciamiento de la obra social”. Y agregó: “Ese sistema de salud que colapsa no solamente deja sin atención a las fuerzas armadas y de seguridad, sino también a las y los trabajadores civiles, con el malestar que conlleva eso. Los salarios no alcanzan para pagar coseguros o acceder a prácticas médicas mínimas, porque la obra social empieza a no cubrirlas. Sostener esa obra social es posible con una buena administración y con la conciencia plena de que estamos defendiendo los derechos del pueblo. Milei plantea no solamente un plan colonizador, sino también un plan entregador de soberanía que solamente puede llevarse a cabo con el sistema privado de obras sociales y sus negocios”.


En el marco del Plan de Lucha que está llevando a cabo ATE en defensa de la Obra Social, se marchó hacia el Ministerio de Defensa nacional para protestar por el cierre de las 31 farmacias propias, los 1450 puestos de trabajo que están en riesgo y la preservación y sostenimiento del patrimonio – hoteles, delegaciones y Auditoría de Facturación de Prestaciones Regional – que se pretende rematar.


La concentración tuvo lugar en la intersección de Avenida Belgrano y Azopardo de la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires, desde donde las y los dirigentes de ATE repudiaron el cierre de áreas clave que permiten no solo facilitar la atención personalizada para miles de usuarios a lo largo y ancho del país sino también que forman parte de los controles del organismo para que funcione de forma adecuada, impidiendo la doble facturación y otras irregularidades.


Es importante subrayar que de concretarse el cierre de los centros médicos, se perjudicará aun más la atención a las y los afiliados ya que no podrán acceder a prestaciones básicas como por ejemplo consultas clínicas o pediátricas. Además, si hubiera cuando retrasos o suspensiones en los pagos a proveedores no habrá posibilidades de acceder a los servicios de salud.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Trabajo para hoy, catástrofes para mañana: políticos impulsan nuevo estudio para licitar la ruta T-720 en el Parque Alerce Costero
content:
A pesar de años de estudios de impacto ambiental que han obligado a rechazar la ruta, la delegación presidencial junto al MOP, insisten en impulsar nuevamente su construcción.

Esta misma semana que está programada una marcha ambiental a nivel nacional en contra del proyecto Dominga (Minera y Portuaria que están licitando para la comuna de Coquimbo en el norte) y también convocada por organizaciones agrupadas en el Bloque Socioambiental de Valdivia en contra de la Carretera T-720 y hacia la inmobiliaria en Bahía Coique entre otras demandas; se reunieron la Delegada Presidencial Vicky Carrasco, el alcalde de Corral Claudio González, el Seremi de Obras públicas Ulises Rivera, el concejal de Corral Juan Galindo y el presidente de la Asociación Comunal de Organizaciones Rurales de La Unión, Gerardo Almonacid Leiva entre otros, justamente a impulsar una nueva mesa técnica para un nuevo estudio de impacto ambiental de la mismisima Carretera T-720 que quieren trazar en medio del Parque Alerce Costero. Para el cual iniciarán estudios durante el 2027, con el fin de licitarla en el 2028.

Vale la pena recalcar, que este proyecto lleva 18 años siendo rechazado. No por capricho ni mero trámite, como mencionan algunos políticos, al respecto de las personas ambientalistas y defensores y defensoras de la tierra, al contrario, la oposición ha sido porque todos los estudios realizados fueron rechazados uno tras otro, por certezas y argumentos científicos contundentes y de alto impacto para el Parque Alerce Costero y el planeta.

Año tras año la estrategia y los discursos acerca de la supuesta necesidad o “urgencia” de la ruta han ido cambiando. Al principio en el 2008 lo mostraron como una idea para mejorar el turismo, llamándole: “Integración para la Nueva Región: Eje para la Integración y el Desarrollo Turístico Sustentable”, dejando entrever, claramente y sin tapujos, las similitudes y concordancias con un proyecto aún más grande para la región: La I.I.R.S.A (Iniciativa para la Integración de la Infraestructura Regional Suramericana).

Organizaciones sociales y ambientales han denunciado desde entonces los resultados devastadores que tendría este gran proyecto que instala a Chile como un país crucial del Eje Sur, para unir la costa del Atlántico con la costa del Pacífico por vía terrestre.

Luego, el discurso político cambia de “necesidad” y el foco es puesto también en la “conectividad” para la zona entre Corral y La Unión. Pero al observar la ruta T-60 y la T-400 se comprueba que la conectividad existe desde hace años. Los tramos de estas dos rutas suman 95,8 kilómetros de distancia entre las comunas.

Desde Corral hay 42.3 kilómetros de distancia para llegar hasta Valdivia por vía terrestre y el camino viejo de La Unión (T-60) tiene 53,5 km hasta Valdivia. Estos caminos ya existentes son la alternativa actual promovida por organizaciones sociales y medioambientales. Pero ambos caminos están en malas condiciones y hoy se mantienen con inversiones de mejoras que poco se ven. Entonces ¿Por qué no mejorar aquellas? Nadie lo entiende.

Si la lógica es la conectividad y cuidar el medio ambiente, lo que científicos y pobladores proponen, es mejorar estos caminos y que no se intervenga uno de los últimos pulmones y regulador natural del agua/calor del territorio y el planeta. Por otro lado, la ruta T-720 tan solo disminuiría a 90.2 el kilometraje, 5,6 kilómetros de diferencia entre las rutas ya existentes.

Sumado a lo anterior, han insistido en mencionar qué está construcción otorgaría oportunidades de trabajo a las personas y fomentaría el progreso para estás comunas, pero la realidad del calentamiento global y por sobre todo, viendo las últimas catástrofes medioambientales, intervenir lugares de la naturaleza fundamentales para el equilibrio, el control de las aguas y el calentamiento, no conviene en ningún caso, sobre todo intervenir en estas magnitudes la naturaleza (I.I.R.S.A), ya que los costos cómo destruir territorios completos y convertirlos en zonas de sacrificio, son posteriores, y están lejos de considerar el cuidado del medio ambiente. Al contrario, en este tipo de intervenciones, las personas terminan sufriendo el impacto con aluviones, sequías, contaminación de las aguas y destrucción del hábitat del territorio (sin considerar aún el impacto para los Alerces endémicos, la flora y la fauna).

Por último, intentan argumentar en la actualidad, con esta nueva licitación, que ésta sería una demanda de las comunidades …

author: anred
title: BDS reclama a Lula que rompa los vínculos económicos y militares con Israel: «es hora de pasar de las palabras a los hechos”
content:
Imagen: @cois4ruim


La reelección de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva en Brasil generó expectativas en el movimiento internacional de solidaridad con Palestina, pero también reabrió el debate sobre la continuidad de los vínculos económicos, comerciales y militares entre Brasil e Israel. Andressa Oliveira Soares, co-coordinadora de políticas para América Latina del Comité Nacional Palestino del movimiento de Boicot, Desinversión y Sanciones (BDS), calificó el resultado electoral como “una pequeña gota de esperanza”, aunque reclamó que el próximo mandato traduzca las declaraciones diplomáticas en medidas concretas contra Israel. “Brasil ha frustrado los planes imperialistas de Estados Unidos en la región. Ahora, Brasil debe poner su peso geopolítico y económico al servicio de la defensa del derecho internacional”, sostuvo. Entre las principales exigencias, planteó interrumpir las exportaciones de petróleo a Israel, terminar los contratos militares, cancelar el tratado de libre comercio entre el Mercosur e Israel y suspender las importaciones de agrotóxicos, además de cortar los vínculos académicos, deportivos y culturales, por el genocidio que lleva adelante el gobierno de Benjamin Netanyahu contra el pueblo palestino en Gaza.

Por ANRed.


La

reelección de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva para su cuarto mandato en Brasil

 abrió nuevas expectativas y también exigencias en el movimiento internacional de solidaridad con Palestina. En un pronunciamiento difundido el lunes 26 de octubre, el

Comité Nacional Palestino del movimiento de Boicot, Desinversión y Sanciones (BDS)

planteó que el nuevo mandato presidencial

debe traducir las posiciones diplomáticas de Brasil contra el genocidio en Gaza en medidas concretas contra Israel

.


“La reelección de Lula en Brasil representa para Palestina una pequeña gota de esperanza para quienes creen en la justicia social y los derechos humanos en Latinoamérica y más allá.

El pueblo brasileño ha rechazado contundentemente a la ultraderecha, que en toda América Latina ha avanzado para fortalecer su alianza con el genocida Israel

. Brasil ha frustrado los planes imperialistas de Estados Unidos en la región. Ahora,

Brasil debe poner su peso geopolítico y económico al servicio de la defensa del derecho internacional

. Esta victoria debe traducirse en acciones decisivas en apoyo del derecho internacional para los pueblos oprimidos, desde Palestina hasta Brasil”, remarca el documento, que lleva la firma de

Andressa Oliveira Soares

, co-coordinadora de políticas para América Latina del movimiento.


El pronunciamiento reconoce las posiciones que Lula y sus anteriores gobiernos sostuvieron respecto de Palestina, pero advierte sobre la distancia entre esas declaraciones y las políticas económicas y comerciales: “

los gobiernos previos de Lula han sido favorables al reconocimiento de algunos derechos del pueblo palestino y se han manifestado contra el genocidio

. Sin embargo,

 aún no han dado pasos concretos para imponer sanciones legales efectivas a Israel, tal como lo estableció la Corte Internacional de Justicia

”, en referencia a las medidas provisionales dictadas en el proceso iniciado por Sudáfrica contra Israel por violaciones de la Convención para la Prevención y la Sanción del Delito de Genocidio.


En su momento,

Lula calificó de genocidio las acciones israelíes contra la población palestina y en septiembre de 2025 anunció que Brasil intervendría en el proceso iniciado por Sudáfrica ante la Corte Internacional de Justicia

. El 17 de septiembre de ese año, el país presentó formalmente una declaración de intervención en virtud del artículo 63 del Estatuto de la Corte, en tanto Estado firmante de la Convención contra el Genocidio. Sin embargo,

estas decisiones no implicaron una ruptura de las relaciones diplomáticas ni la suspensión integral de los vínculos comerciales con Israel

.


Uno de los principales puntos señalados por BDS es la continuidad del intercambio económico

. El tratado de libre comercio entre el Mercosur e Israel, firmado en 2007 y vigente para Brasil desde abril de 2010, continúa en funcionamiento. Según datos del Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores brasileño, el intercambio comercial bilateral alcanzó los 1.900 millones de dólares durante 2025: Brasil exportó bienes por 568,6 millones e importó aproximadamente 1.300 millones.
