author: Rizomatica
title: Documental sobre el estallido social dirigido por María Teresa Larraín llega a la UCT el 5 de noviembre
content:
Cuerpos en Crisis sigue a cinco activistas durante el estallido social de 2019 y el proceso constituyente de 2021-2022 en Chile. La función es de entrada liberada y contará con un conversatorio abierto a la comunidad.


El jueves 5 de noviembre, a las 17:00 hrs, se presentará en Temuco Cuerpos en Crisis, el nuevo documental de la cineasta chileno-canadiense María Teresa Larraín. La actividad, de entrada liberada, se realizará en el Auditorio H2 del Campus San Francisco de la Universidad Católica de Temuco y es organizada por el Observatorio Ciudadano, con el patrocinio del Departamento de Sociología, Ciencia Política y Administración Pública de la UCT.


Tras la exhibición habrá un conversatorio con la directora y con la abogada y ex convencional constituyente mapuche Rosa Catrileo, moderado por Mabel Cobos, codirectora del Observatorio Ciudadano.


La película registra el estallido social de 2019 y el proceso constituyente a través de cinco activistas de los movimientos de la discapacidad, migrantes, diversidades sexo-genéricas y personas privadas de libertad. También participan integrantes de la Convención Constitucional, entre ellos tres mujeres indígenas, y personas que filmaron las calles con imágenes que nunca llegaron a la prensa oficial.


Larraín, ciega y residente en Toronto, dejó Chile tras el golpe de Estado de 1973. Comenzó a perder la vista durante el montaje de un documental anterior. Su primer largometraje independiente fue El Juicio de Pascual Pichun (2007), que retrata la historia de dos familias, la del lonko Pascual Pichun y la del terrateniente Agustín Figueroa, en lo que se conoció como uno de los juicios más emblemáticos de la historia de Chile. Su obra posterior incluye Niña Sombra (2016), sobre los vendedores ambulantes ciegos de la Alameda.


“Esta película es mi respuesta. Un homenaje a quienes perdieron la vida defendiendo un proceso transformador que me marcó para siempre”, afirma la directora.


Estrenada en 2025, Cuerpos en Crisis obtuvo el Premio a Mejor Film de la Diáspora en el Toronto International Nollywood Film Festival 2025, donde además fue nominada a Mejor Documental de Canadá, y fue nominada a Mejor Documental de Derechos Humanos en el Montreal Independent Film Festival 2026.


Tras su paso por Toronto y México, la película recorre Chile antes de su lanzamiento oficial en Sala K de Santiago el 27 de noviembre. En la región, además de Temuco, se exhibirá el 6 de noviembre en Saavedra (Ruka y Huerto Llelliuken, con integrantes de la comunidad mapuche KOLWE) y el 7 en Curarrehue (Aldea Intercultural Trawupeyüm).

author: Administrador
title: Preparativos Zapatistas para el Encuentro Abrazo con familias Buscadoras. Parte 3: CUIDAR, PROTEGER, GUARDAR
content:
Música: Meme del Real, «El mundo en que nací» Imágenes, edición y producción: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

Compañeras Familias Buscadoras:

Les saluda el Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés, coordinador general de la Gira por la Vida – Capítulo México.

Pues les comento que seguimos preparándonos para el viaje que haremos para conocerlas, y escuchar y aprender de sus dolores y resistencia. Y para guardar su palabra en nuestros corazones y en nuestra memoria. Esperamos, de veras, aprender mucho de ustedes.

Acá donde estamos concentrados, de repente llueve mucho y hace frío. Está bien para quienes vienen en tierras frías, pero los de tierra caliente, pues sufren un poco porque no están hallados. A la lluvia todos estamos bien hallados, porque de por sí acá en las montañas del sureste mexicano llueve mucho. Montaña adentro, en las lomas y la selva, llueve hasta cuando no llueve.

Unas con frío, otras con calor, las comunidades zapatistas han mandado a prepararse a delegadas, delegados y 3 delegadoas. Hasta ahora 1530 según la cuenta. Tal vez baja la cantidad por enfermedades o asuntos familiares. Por ejemplo, una compañera se sintió mal, la atendieron y salió en el ultrasonido que trae cría en su panza. Tuvo que regresar, por razón de que estén bien ella y su pichito. Pero rápido, un compañero que le sabe a eso de los tacos (de hacerlos, no de comerlos; porque de comerlos todos, todas y todoas estamos muy bien entrenados), rápido dijo que él entra de relevo. Y sí lo aprobaron las comandantas y comandantes porque de por sí escucha las pláticas que se dan para prepararnos bien.

Aquí en el video les mostramos unas de nuestras preparaciones.

Sea toda la delegación completa, sea en las partes en que nos organizamos, nos preparamos para marchas si es que hay o para mítines que les dicen. En esas marchas, si es que se hacen, nuestra principal preocupación no es el rollo que digamos, sino cuidar, guardar y proteger a las familias buscadoras. O sea que no vamos a la bulla, a echar relajo, sino a escuchar su palabra. Y pues tenemos que ver de cuidarlas porque en su corazón tienen palabras fuertes, duras, que enseñan y orientan en la lucha por la vida.

Y sabemos que aprenderemos porque llevamos nuestra libreta y nuestro lapicero. Y hasta computadoras y tabletas y celulares. Y van compañeras que les decimos “Tercias Compas” que le saben a eso de la cámara, la grabación, la edición y la transmisión de los encuentros. Pero lo más importante es que llevamos la cabeza, el corazón y las tripas con ganas de aprender.

Ahí pueden ver, en el video, que se ponen unas compañeras con sus pichitos como si fueran familias buscadoras marchando por verdad y justicia, y luego nuestra delegación o parte de nuestra delegación, camina a su lado y luego las envuelve en un como escudo.

Y hasta el Comando Palomitas practica de hacer el escudo que cuida, protege y guarda.

De por sí así nos enseñaron nuestros anteriores, que nos dijeron que somos guardianes y guardianas de la tierra, la madre más primera.

Como ven en las imágenes, con tanto lodo que se hace en las prácticas pues ya casi no es que marchamos, sino que como que nos deslizamos. Como patinando pues. Y luego pasa pues que la chancla se quedó atorada, o el tenis, y no se puede parar porque atrás viene la bola, el bulto de compas. Y entonces pues ni modos, hay que esperar a que termina la práctica para ir a buscar en el lodo, dónde es que quedó la chancla o el tenis. Y pues mientras andamos como chuchito renco.

Compañeras familias buscadoras:

No vamos a pasear. Vamos a abrazarlas si quieren, y si no, pues también vamos para oír su palabra.

Lo sabemos que hay gente que está mal hablando de la gira. Dividen, quieren decir quién sí y quién no puede reunirse con nosotros, o sea que quieren dejar fuera a otros grupos porque no se llevan, y cosas así. Ahí después, otro día, el Capitán Marcos les va a decir de eso hasta con nombres.

Por ahora sólo queremos mandarles nuestros respetos y cariño.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano. Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. México, octubre del 2026.

author: Aldrey Olegario
title: ‘Primavera Brasileira’: como ato de estudantes virou onda global contra extrema direita
content:
Na noite de 4 de outubro, quando Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) terminou à frente de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) no 1.º turno das eleições, a seguinte mensagem chegou num grupo de WhatsApp de alunos da Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF): “O momento pede ação”. Na noite seguinte, 5 de outubro, o Brasil assistiu ao primeiro ato dos jovens.


“Nós vimos a vitória do Flávio de uma forma muito acachapante. Ninguém estava esperando. Aquilo gerou um sentimento de descrença muito forte no campo progressista. Mas na Faculdade de Direito da UFF, pela nossa história, enxergamos de forma contrária: com esperança e com vontade de ir à luta”, diz Kayky Moraes, aluno do curso de direito da UFF que participou do primeiro levante.


Realizada em Niterói, na região metropolitana do Rio de Janeiro, a marcha dos estudantes saiu do prédio da Faculdade de Direito rumo à reitoria da universidade.

As imagens tomaram as redes e iniciaram um efeito dominó que impulsionou mobilizações estudantis nos cinco cantos do país. “Ali a gente sentiu que dava para brigar.”


Neste momento manifestação contra Bolsonaro pelos estudantes nas ruas Niterói

pic.twitter.com/7sqGGEq7TV

— Fã do Rei Pelé e da Rainha Marta


 (@silvaS1963)

October 5, 2026


O resultado desse “efeito borboleta” veio no dia 25 de outubro, três semanas depois. Um feito histórico: Lula virou o jogo e

venceu as eleições

 por uma vantagem de 4,4 milhões de votos, algo que nenhum candidato a presidente que terminou como segundo colocado no 1º turno havia conseguido fazer antes. Os eleitores de Lula e os estrategistas de campanha do PT tiveram apenas três semanas para mudar a rota. “Essa foi a campanha menos organizada que participei desde 1989”, chegou a dizer o presidente Lula em uma reunião com parlamentares em Brasília.


“Os jovens tomaram as ruas de forma orgânica e organizada para defender um projeto de país, mas também um projeto de ser humano. Quando Lula disse aquela frase para a gente ser ele amanhã, porque ele já foi a gente ontem e para a juventude botar a cara a tapa, acho que é isso mesmo”, diz Kayky, em referência a um trecho da entrevista de Lula para o podcast Flow.

“Estamos fadados a viver o futuro e a gente tem que construir o futuro que a gente quer.”


A “primavera brasileira”, como começou a ser apelidada a vitória eleitoral frente à extrema direita, também pode ser vista por como uma posição do Brasil

como símbolo de resistência aos interesses dos Estados Unidos, defende Mayra Goulart, doutora em ciência política pela UERJ.


“O Brasil será um pólo da resistência à relação imperial que os Estados Unidos tentam restabelecer. Na última assembleia geral da ONU, Lula disse que o Brasil não iria ser o quintal de ninguém. O presidente Lula recupera a tradição de não alinhamento automático da diplomacia brasileira a potências estrangeiras e a adoção de um caminho próprio e soberanista. Isso é entendido muitas vezes como um caminho que vem a liderar outros países periféricos”, diz.


A “Primavera Brasileira” vista do exterior


No México e na Espanha, a virada eleitoral brasileira foi recebida não apenas com alívio geopolítico, mas como um estudo de caso sobre como conter a ascensão da extrema direita.


Para Homero Campa Butrón, cientista político e professor da Universidade Nacional Autônoma do México (UNAM), a manutenção do governo progressista no Brasil evita o isolamento regional no continente. “Brasil e México representam 55% da população da América Latina e 60% da economia da região. O resultado no Brasil foi vital para o governo mexicano, pois evita o isolamento diante da onda de vitórias da direita na região nos últimos meses”, analisa Campa, destacando que a comunicação entre a presidenta mexicana Claudia Sheinbaum e Lula é direta e estratégica.


O impacto também ressoa na Europa. “Se o Brasil conseguiu, a Espanha também consegue”, disse o primeiro-ministro da Espanha Pedro Sánchez

, em um comício em Gijón, na região de Astúrias, realizado na segunda-feira, 26 de outubro. “Vamos fazer o mesmo que Lula fez no Brasil. O mundo está olhando para nós”, completou.


Com eleições gerais agendadas para o próximo mês na Espanha, onde as pesquisas têm indicado a predileção do eleitorado à direita, o desfecho brasileiro renovou o ânimo das forças de esquerda. “Certamente, no México e na Espanha, percebe-se um enorme interesse no modelo de mobilização social promovido por meio das redes sociais, coordenado pelo deputado André Janones. author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: Cuidar la vida en el territorio: la deuda pendiente con las mujeres del campo
content:
OPINIÓN


Por Carolina Llorens*


Las tareas de cuidados recaen de manera desproporcionada sobre las mujeres y disidencias y en el ámbito rural la realidad es aún más compleja. Según datos del Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena Somos Tierra (MNCI ST),

 en Argentina el 60 por ciento de las mujeres rurales vive una triple jornada simultánea: producen alimentos, sostienen el hogar y cuidan del territorio

. En promedio, trabajan más de 14 horas al día, lo que les deja apenas 1,6 horas diarias para el descanso o el autocuidado. Cada 29 de octubre se conmemora el Día Internacional del Cuidado y el Apoyo. Esta fecha, propuesta por las Naciones Unidas en 2023, invita a reflexionar sobre estas tareas que hacen posible la vida, pero que rara vez son reconocidas


Lejos de ser una vocación natural, el cuidado en el campo es un acto político.

Para las comunidades campesinas e indígenas, el cuidado es integral: abarca la tierra, el agua, las semillas criollas, la biodiversidad, los animales y los saberes ancestrales.

Sin embargo, esta labor se desarrolla en un contexto de abandono estatal y crisis climática, donde las mujeres rurales actúan como el "amortiguador" que sostiene la vida en los territorios. El impacto en la salud es alarmante: el 85 por ciento de ellas sufre estrés constante y casi la mitad no acude al médico por falta de tiempo.


Un diagnóstico de desfinanciamiento


Esta realidad rural se enmarca en un escenario nacional crítico. El conjunto de organizaciones que impulsan el

Acuerdo Nacional por los Cuidados

 advierten que en los últimos años se destruyeron 48 de 50 políticas de cuidado, lo que profundizó el abandono y trasladó la carga de manera desproporcionada hacia los hogares y, especialmente, hacia las mujeres. "Hoy la organización social del cuidado está en emergencia", señalan. Mientras el costo de vida aumenta y el hambre crece,

las redes comunitarias intentan cubrir las necesidades básicas

, pero no pueden reemplazar la responsabilidad del Estado.


Para las familias rurales, esta ausencia estatal es doblemente grave. La falta de acceso a salud integral, infraestructuras y servicios básicos, sumada a la falta de regulación de la propiedad comunitaria y a las políticas de adaptación al cambio climático, coloca a las mujeres del campo en una situación de extrema vulnerabilidad. La sobrecarga de trabajo no solo limita su autonomía, sino que también se constituye como una forma de violencia estructural.


Foto: MNCI ST


Hacia un Acuerdo Nacional por los Cuidados


El Acuerdo Nacional por los Cuidados, respaldado por una amplia diversidad de organizaciones sociales, sindicatos y académicos, plantea la necesidad de reconstruir una organización social del cuidado basada en la corresponsabilidad. Esto implica que el Estado, las familias, las comunidades, los sindicatos y el sector privado asuman responsabilidades concretas.


La propuesta no se limita a un conjunto de políticas aisladas, sino que busca ser un proyecto de país que ponga la sostenibilidad de la vida en el centro de la agenda pública.


Desde el sector rural se impulsa a que este acuerdo nacional tenga una perspectiva campesina, indígena y territorial. Para las mujeres rurales, esto se traduce en exigencias urgentes: acceso a la salud, servicios básicos, regulación de la propiedad comunitaria, reconocimiento del cuidado comunitario rural como un trabajo y políticas de adaptación al cambio climático que garanticen agua, alimentos y condiciones dignas para vivir y producir.


La urgencia de esta demanda radica en que el cuidado no puede seguir siendo una responsabilidad individual ni recaer siempre sobre las mujeres y diversidades.

 Construir un sistema integral de cuidados es una inversión estratégica que no solo mejora la calidad de vida de quienes cuidan, sino que también dinamiza la economía y reduce las desigualdades. En el campo, donde las mujeres sostienen la producción de alimentos y la biodiversidad, garantizar el derecho al cuidado es garantizar la soberanía alimentaria y el arraigo.


Porque cuidar debe ser un proyecto de país, en el Día Internacional de los Cuidados, la voz de las mujeres y diversidades rurales se alza para exigir que el Estado deje de mirar para otro lado y reconozca que, sin cuidados, no hay vida posible en los territorios.


*Coordinadora del Equipo de Feminismo y Diversidades del Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena - Somos Tierra

author: Brian Hioe
title: Pakistan Abruptly Cancels Taiwanese Overflight Routes Then Reverses Course
content:
IN AN UNUSUAL series of events, in short order, Pakistan declared that Taiwanese airlines would not be allowed to fly over the country, then reversed course on the decision.

The decision was announced by Pakistan’s Minister of Defense Khawaja Asif, who stated that the new policy was made to comply with Pakistan’s One China Policy. Originally, Taiwanese airlines EVA Air and China Airlines had been cleared for overflight privileges by Pakistan from October 28 of this year through March 27, 2027, as approved by the country’s Civil Aviation Authority.

This would be the first time that a country has revoked overflight privileges for Taiwanese air carriers, on the basis of a claimed One China Policy. If so, it could be that Pakistan would be seeking closer ties with China, and hitting out at Taiwan would be a means of doing so. Or Pakistan could have been acting on China’s behest, with China expected to try and constrain Taiwan’s international space ahead of the upcoming local elections next month. As for why Pakistan later reversed course, this is also unclear, except perhaps that international backlash was larger than expected–or perhaps there was pressure behind the scenes from the US.

This is not the only time that similar events have occurred in recent memory, however. Earlier this year, a planned trip by President Lai Ching-te to Eswatini, Taiwan’s only African diplomatic ally, to mark King Mswati III’s 40th anniversary of accession to the throne, as well as Mswati’s 58th birthday, was abruptly cancelled. Specifically, countries that Lai would have passed over on his flight to Eswatini, Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles revoked overflight permissions shortly before Lai was to set out on his trip.

The sudden cancellation was largely interpreted as China flexing its muscles in terms of its influence in Africa, with the Lai administration suggesting that China threatened to revoke debt cancellation for Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles if they did not comply. It is unclear, then, whether something similar could have occurred with Pakistan, in that the attempt to revoke overflight privileges could have occurred because of Chinese pressure, but also could have occurred as a result of actions by the Pakistani government.

It is to be seen if this is a new tactic in China’s playbook, then, seeking to limit travel by Taiwanese airlines as a sign of Chinese displeasure. Still, such actions may ultimately anger Taiwan, reminding the public shortly before elections of Chinese coercion and its bullying on the international stage. One may perhaps perceive reports of Taiwanese having their passports confiscated by Ugandan and Kenyan authorities with the demand to provide Chinese travel documents in a similar vein, even if Kenya later reversed course. This, too, could occur at the initiative of these countries’ governments or because of Chinese pressure, with China using its substantial economic and political heft globally in order for this to occur.

author: groundxero
title: With ‘Largest Coordinated Port Action Ever,’ Dockworkers in 22 Countries Strike Against Gaza Genocide
content:
“We, the workers in the ports, know very well that without us nothing moves. Without our hands, containers remain still, ships are not loaded, the war machines are blocked.”


 


Jake Johnson


Oct 30, 2026


 


Dockworkers in more than 20 countries—from

France

 to India to Greece—are withholding their labor on Friday to demand an end to Israel’s genocidal assault on

Gaza

 and highlight the role that commercial ports play in fueling deadly

militarism

 worldwide.


 


Organizers said the work stoppages, led by dockworkers’

unions

 at

113 ports across 22 countries

, would be the “largest coordinated port action ever,” easily surpassing the international day of action held in February. No Harbour for

Genocide

, a collective of

trade

 unions and others supporting the day of action, said $2.8 billion worth of cargo will be halted at Mediterranean ports, where

workers

 are planning to strike for 24 hours.


 


“A cargo refused in one port sails on to the next,” said No Harbour for Genocide. “Refused in every port, it stops, and the workers have enforced the embargo that governments announced and did not.”


 


In a

joint statement

 last month announcing the day of action, dockworkers’ unions from Türkiye, Morocco, Italy, France,

Greece

, Italy, and Basque Country laid out their demands:


 


An immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and the opening of safe corridor for

humanitarian aid

.. An end of colonization, occupation and

apartheid

 imposed to Palestinian People and the recognition of an independent Palestinian state recognized by the international community on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.


 


An end to the war in the Middle East. No support, no facilitation, no participation in the US-Israeli war against Iran,

Lebanon

 or any other imperialist intervention. Military fleets and bases out of the region. We express our full

solidarity

 to the people of

Cuba

 and

Venezuela

 and

Sudan

 menaced by US

imperialism

 and we call for defend people’s sovereignty, resources, territorial integrity, peace with justice, and the right for resistance for self-determination.


 


Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops. We call on unions to strengthen vigilance, to inform workers, to expose the cargoes of war, and to organize mass collective resistance with all our rightful available means and our struggle.


 


An end to the

militarization

 of ports and critical

infrastructure

. Ports belong to the peoples and the workers. They are not bases for

NATO

, the USA or the EU, nor tools of shipowners and monopoly groups.


 


No to the war economy and armaments. The money must go to wages, collective agreements, health, education, social needs, and the protection of life and safety at work.


 


Health and safety measures in the workplaces. Not one worker dead for profits. An end to intensification, subcontracting, dangerous conditions, and employer arbitrariness.


 


Collective agreements with real wage increases, stable jobs with rights, a retirement policy with better pensions, and a reduction of working time. Technological developments, mechanization, automation, the use of AI and the development of ports must serve the needs of workers, and not lead to the intensification of work or the disappearance of their jobs.


 


“Our strength lies in organization. It lies in our unions, in general assemblies, in collective decisions, in solidarity among workers from different countries,” the unions said. “We, the workers in the ports, know very well that without us nothing moves. Without our hands, containers remain still, ships are not loaded, the war machines are blocked.”


 


Al Jazeera

noted

 that of the ports participating in Friday’s actions, “Genoa, Livorno, and Gioia Tauro in Italy, Marseille in France, Piraeus in Greece, and Tangier in Morocco all have proven links to weapons shipments to Israel.”


Dockworkers International Day of Action across 5 Continents and 113 Ports


In Pireaus, at COSCO’s terminals, dockworkers are holding the picket lines. Their message is clear


Dockworkers do not work for war! Ports for the peoples and for peace, not bases for imperialists!

pic.twitter.com/cpOwK8XLhV


— PAME Greece International (@PAME_Greece)

October 30, 2026


The strikes come as Israel’s genocide in

title: Hegseth visit exposes deepening US military intervention in the Philippines
content:
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth attends a meeting in Cebu on October 28, 2026, together with other defense leaders from other countries. Photo from the Department of National Defense's Facebook page

For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.

The arrival of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in Cebu on October 28 has drawn condemnation from progressive groups, which warned that the Philippines is increasingly being drawn into Washington’s military and economic agenda at the expense of national sovereignty.

The International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines said Hegseth’s visit for the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting comes amid the Trump administration’s aggressive expansion of US military power in the Asia-Pacific and its preparations for greater confrontation with China.

The group described Hegseth as a key enforcer of Washington’s war agenda, criticizing Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration for facilitating the growing US military presence in the country.

Under the Marcos administration, military cooperation between Manila and Washington has expanded through weapons deployments, joint military exercises, intelligence-sharing arrangements, and the increased use of Philippine military facilities.

Read: Missiles, markets, and massacres: Balikatan, ASEAN, and the war logic of US imperial decline*

During Hegseth’s March 2025 visit, the two governments agreed to deploy advanced US weapons, including the Navy Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS), expand high-end military exercises, strengthen defense-industrial cooperation, and launch joint cyber operations.

In October 2025, Hegseth and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. announced a Task Force-Philippines to strengthen joint military planning and operational coordination. This was followed by a 15-year Communications Interoperability and Security Memorandum of Agreement (CISMOA) in May 2026, further institutionalizing secure military communications and information-sharing between the two countries.

These arrangements build on the General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA) and the nine Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) sites across the Philippines.

For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.

The consequences, the group warned, extend beyond military installations. With US forces increasingly capable of operating advanced weapons from Philippine territory, Filipino communities could become vulnerable to retaliation in the event of a regional conflict.

Read: Tacloban fishers slam Balikatan exercises

During the May 2026 Balikatan exercises, the US military reportedly launched a Tomahawk cruise missile from Tacloban Airport, demonstrating its capacity to conduct long-range missile strikes from Philippine soil.

“Our country is being transformed into a forward operating platform for US wars, exposing millions of Filipinos to the grave danger of retaliation, devastation, and death in a regional conflict,” ILPS Philippines said.

The group accused the Marcos administration of sacrificing national independence through its cooperation with Washington, using tensions with China to justify the expanding US military footprint.

While opposing China’s coercion and violations of Philippine sovereign rights, ILPS Philippines stressed that the country cannot defend its sovereignty by allowing another foreign power to use its territory for military operations and war preparations.

Progressive groups also warned that US intervention is not confined to military installations. They said Washington’s economic initiatives are tied to its strategic interests in the Philippines, particularly its access to critical resources and supply chains.

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) condemned Hegseth’s visit, saying the US is pursuing both military access and greater control over resources through initiatives such as Pax Silica.

A US-led initiative seeking to secure supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other strategic technologies, Pax Silica could further open Philippine resources to foreign corporate interests, the farmers’ group warned.

author: Kodao Productions
title: IBON’s Africa schools Marcos on why peso, economy are weak
content:
Contrary to his assurances that there is no need to panic, Philippines’ Ferdinand Marcos Jr. should start worrying, independent economist Sonny Africa said. Africa said the president should take a deep look as to why the value of the Philippine peso has taken a dive never before seen in the country’s history.


Africa said Marcos should stop blaming geopolitical pressures alone, such as the war in the Middle East, why the peso is currently the worst performing currency in Southeast Asia.


In an interview with reporters on Wednesday, Marcos urged Filipinos not to panic as the country’s currency breached P64 per US dollar several times this week, assuring the public that his government has the tools and reserves to keep the economy afloat.


Marcos said that the Philippines’ foreign exchange reserves are healthy enough to defend the peso. The president blamed the currency slide and broader price pressures to supply-side factors, especially oil and energy, due to the ongoing war in the Middle East.


“Oil we can do nothing about. Food, we can,” he said, assuring that the administration is working on ways to bring down food prices and ease the burden on Filipino consumers.


Africa, however, said the president’s words are not having their intended effects as the Philippines labors under its steepest inflation rate this year at 7.2 per cent.


Energy bill woes for common folks


Erna Basinal was surprised at the spike in their electricity bill for October that grew by at least 30 per cent, from less than P4,000 in September to more than P6,000 this month.


“We do not know where else to find money to pay this,” she said, citing her husband’s monthly pension as a retired office clerk could no longer cover their living costs.


Last October 9, the ERC approved a transmission cost hike of P1.48 per kilowatt hour for power distribution company Meralco, the country’s largest, causing similar reactions from 8.2 households and businesses across the company’s franchise area.


Reality bites


Marcos’ own technocrats are not as optimistic as well, such as his energy secretary who told reporters at the sidelines of the Singapore International Energy Week: “This is not the best time to be secretary.”


Energy secretary Sharon Garin warned that the weakened peso is driving up the cost of imported coal, diesel and liquefied natural gas the country mostly depends on for electricity generation. The diving peso adds pressure on electricity rates and fuel pump prices at a time when the country is also grappling with high global oil prices and the threat of El Niño, she said.


Garin said she would soon meet with the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to find ways to cushion the impact of the peso depreciation and continued market volatility.


Where is the peso’s weakness from?


While the war in the Middle East could be blamed for instigating the peso’s dive, Africa said Marcos should stop blaming geopolitical conflicts alone for the country’s woes.


“The peso is weak because the economy is weak. We need more and more dollars to import what we don’t produce, but produce less and less to export and earn dollars from,” Aftica said.


He said Marcos should be blamed for his lack of support to Philippine agriculture, allowing the country to import US$20 billion in food and agricultural products while exporting just US$9.3 billion in return. He added that the Philippines also suffers trade imbalance in consumer goods.


The one thing that Africa agrees with Marcos is the role of overseas Filipino workers in keeping the Philippines afloat with US$40 billion in annual remittance.


The IBON Foundation executive director added: “Even more panic-inducing to Filipinos is the president saying not to panic, while still not really doing anything to help all the millions of families being driven into deeper distress and crisis.”


Africa said Marcos should pour more resources for rural development to encourage greater agricultural production and stop Philippine dependence on imports. He also encouraged national industrialization to stem expenditures on commodity imports.


“The fault isn’t in the short-term factors being blamed like the US attack on Iran driving up oil prices. It’s in the long neglect of strengthening domestic agriculture and Filipino industry,” he said.


“Filipinos have reason to panic. As things are, food prices and inflation look set to get even worse through Christmas and coming into the New Year,” Africa concluded. # …

author: Daniel Aloc
title: Ganggang ni JL Burgos bilang salamin ng lipunan
content:
Natatangi ang karanasan ng mga batang lumalaki sa kanayunan, malayo sa kalunsuran na may madaling access sa teknolohiya. Sa pagitan ng pagpasok sa paaralan at paglalaro sa mga burol at parang—kabilang na ang paghahanap ng mga gagambang panlaban sa kapwa gagamba—unti-unti nilang natututuhan ang mga realidad ng mundong kanyang ginagalawan. May nananalo, may natatalo; may nambubully, at may napipilitan lumaban upang hindi na lamang manatiling api.

Ngunit paano kung ang mga larong kinalakihan nila ay naging daan upang maaga silang mamulat sa karahasang umiiral sa lipunan? Paano kung ang mga batang dapat sana ay malayang naglalaro ay maagang nahaharap sa dahas, takot, at pang-aabuso.

Ilan lamang ito sa mga tanong na sinisikap sagutin ng Ganggang, ang kauna-unahang full-length narrative film ni JL Burgos, na unang ipinalabas sa Cinemalaya noong Agosto. Nitong Oktubre 21 ko lamang ito napanood sa Cinematheque Centre Manila, na ngayo’y matatagpuan sa bagong tahanan nito sa Philippine Film Heritage Building sa Intramuros, bilang bahagi ng Pelikula ng Bayan: Cinemalaya 22.

Hindi na katakataka ang tema at paksang tinatalakay ng pelikula, lalo na’t ang gumawa nito ay isang filmmaker na matagal nang nakatuon sa usapin ng karapatang pantao. Bago ang Ganggang, nakilala na si Burgos sa mga dokumentaryong Portraits of Mosquito Press at Alipato at Muog (2024). Ang huli ay nagwagi ng Best Picture, Best Documentary, at Best Editing sa ika-48 Gawad Urian noong 2025.

Hindi isang bagong proyektong biglaang nabuo ang Ganggang kasunod ng tagumpay ng Alipato at Muog. Ayon kay Burgos, isinulat niya ang kwento noon pang 2019. Sa halip na talikuran ang mga isyung matagal na niyang tinalakay sa kanyang mga dokumentaryo, pinili niyang ilahad ang mga ito sa pamamagitan ng naratibo ng isang pelikula—sa lente ng mga batang hindi pa lubusang nauunawaan ang bigat ng mga puwersang humuhubog sa kanilang buhay.

Sa pelikula, sina Ilay (Kenneth “Butchoy” Vincent Mendoza), Ten-ten (Don Rishmond Cerbito), at Mel (Raine Dela Cruz) ay tatlong batang naging magkaibigan sa paghahanap ng gagambang panlaban sa gagamba ni Anton (Prince Nathaniel España), ang bully sa kanilang paaralan. May kanya-kanyang pinagmulan ang tatlong bata. Anak ng isang desaparecido si Ilay, anak ng magsasaka si Ten-ten, at anak na naman ng isang sundalo si Mel.

Sa unang tingin, ang Ganggang ay isang pamilyar na bahagi ng pagkabata sa maraming pamayanan sa bansa. May tuwa sa paghahanap ng gagamba at sa pananabik na makita kung alin ang mananaig. Ngunit isa itong alegorya ng isang lipunang tila nakondisyon nang maniwala na kailangang maglaban-laban ang mamamayan upang mabuhay.

Sa talkback at Q&A session matapos ang screening, ipinaliwanag ni Burgos ang kahulugan ng tunggalian ng mga gagamba. Hindi naman likas sa mga ito ang mag-away sa paraang nakikita sa laro; inilalagay sila ng tao sa sitwasyong kailangan nilang magpatayan. Katulad ng mga mamamayang napipilitang mag-unahan at maglaban sa isang sistemang pinaghaharian ng iilan.

Sentrong usapin ng pelikula ang militarisasyon sa kanayunan. Binabago ng presensya ng mga sundalo ang pang-araw-araw na buhay ng mga residente, kabilang ang mga guro at magsasakang itinuturing na mga miyembro o tagasuporta ng New People’s Army (NPA) dahil lamang sa kanilang mga paninindigan.

Bukod sa karahasan at paglabag sa karapatang pantao na iniuugnay sa estado, ipinakikita rin nito ang epekto ng karahasan sa mga bata at kanilang pamilya.

Mahalagang banggitin na ang ilan sa mga karakter at eksena sa pelikula ay hango sa mga tunay na tao at pangyayari.

Isa rito si Rebelyn, ang gurong karakter sa pelikula na hango kay Rebelyn Pitao, anak ni Leoncio Pitao, na mas kilala bilang Commander Parago ng NPA sa Davao. Noong 2009, dinukot si Rebelyn at natagpuan ang kanyang bangkay kinabukasan. Ayon sa ulat ng Commission on Human Rights, ang biktima ay may mga saksak sa dibdib at iba pang palatandaan ng matinding tortyur. Ang sinapit ni Rebelyn ay isang paalala na ang mga taong hindi naman aktwal na nakikidigma ay maaari pa ring maging target ng estado.

Ang plaka naman ng sasakyang ipinakikita sa unang bahagi ng pelikula ay kapareho ng plaka ng sasakyang ginamit sa pagdukot sa kapatid ng direktor na si Jonas Burgos sa isang mall sa Quezon City noong 2007. Hanggang ngayon, hindi pa natatagpuan si Jonas.

Hango rin sa mga tunay na pangyayari ang eksenang nire-red-tag ng isang opisyal ng militar ang gurong si Rebelyn at ang kaniyang mga kasama bilang mga rebelde …

author: rti_admin
title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. The first concerns the content and …

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. author: Unknown
title: From France to Kurdistan: How well do we understand society in transition?
content:
France occupies a special place in the political memory of the modern world. The Enlightenment, the Revolution of 1789, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen gave freedom and equality universal significance. Yet proclaiming rights does not necessarily mean that all social groups can exercise them equally. The Republic’s promise of equality has repeatedly been put to the test by colonialism, class divisions, and discrimination against citizens with migrant backgrounds.


Against this backdrop, the words of jurist and statesman Robert Badinter, who lost his father during the Nazi occupation and played a key role in abolishing the death penalty in 1981, take on particular significance: “France is not the country of human rights, but the country where the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was proclaimed.” The gap between the historical legacy of these rights and contemporary social realities continues to demand critical examination.


The new language of the streets


The protests by students at French secondary schools, which began in mid-September and continued throughout October 2026, offer valuable insights into contemporary French society. Teacher shortages, long school days, overcrowded classrooms, poor conditions in school cafeterias, and anxieties about the future are among the students’ concerns. Some protest signs also reveal a sense of humor: the irony of a student complaining that his overloaded timetable leaves him no time to see his girlfriend may seem trivial at first glance. Yet these young people are questioning not only the conditions of their education but also the way their everyday lives are organized.


After five weeks of sustained protests, the government announced a plan on October 26 that included changes to the Parcoursup* higher education admissions system, reductions in class sizes, and the creation of additional university places. School and university student organizations considered these measures insufficient. The fact that problems raised for years only make it onto the political agenda following mass mobilization by young people highlights the difference between merely listening to the youth and genuinely responding to their demands.


Taking to the streets is nothing new in France. The country has a deeply rooted culture of protest, stretching from the revolutions and May 1968 to workers’ strikes and demonstrations against pension reforms. Today’s Generation Z, however, has a different relationship with traditional institutions. Digital communication tools make it easier to mobilize around specific demands in a very short time. Yet this is not simply a matter of new means of organization. Young people refuse to let others determine their lives and futures. They demand that their voices, living conditions, and expectations be taken seriously, and they want to play an active role in shaping their own future.


How well do we, who are intimately familiar with May 1968 and the political struggles of the past, truly know today’s French youth and the social realities in which they live?


We live in an age when access to information is easier than ever before. Yet having access to information is far from the same as understanding society as it is lived today. Young people who do not carry the political memory of previous generations can still fight against the injustices they experience themselves. Rather than judging them by the standards of the past, we must listen to them and understand what they have to say today.


Between solidarity and racist violence


The social reality of France cannot be understood solely through young people’s protests and their search for solidarity. In a country where the ideals of freedom and equality have a significant historical legacy, discrimination, exclusion, and racist violence also persist.


After the protests by secondary school students had dominated public debate, an armed attack in Trappes and La Verrière on October 23 once again brought another, darker side of France into focus. One person was killed and five others were injured, including a twelve-year-old child. President Emmanuel Macron described the incident as a “racist terrorist attack.” Investigations are underway on suspicion of a racist motive and terrorist offenses.


No direct causal link can be established between the students’ protests against their educational conditions and this attack. However, the fact that both occurred during the same …

author: Syafiq Fadli, Cheong Huei Ting
title: States refuse to act on South East Asia’s transboundary haze
content:
The recent State of Global Air report published by the Health Effects Institute and published on the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service website, identified Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania as the region with the fourth-highest death rates attributable to air pollution, at 100 deaths per 100,000 people.

The World Health Organization reports that “when inhaled, health-damaging pollutants including small particulates can penetrate deep into the respiratory system and enter the bloodstream, allowing them to reach almost all organs within the body, including but not limited to cardiovascular, reproductive and metabolic systems, brain, liver and kidneys.”

The wildfires in parts of Indonesia, which started in early September, have impacted communities across South East Asia. Malaysian climate activists Syafiq Fadli and Huei Ting Cheong look at the origins of this toxic air pollution and why governments still refuse to take serious action to protect lives.

Transboundary haze has been a recurring environmental issue in Malaysia and the Southeast Asia region since the late 1990s, caused by slash-and-burn land clearing methods to cultivate palm oil plantations and a highly humid tropical climate with temperature fluctuations. It is a form of air pollution characterised by fine particles in the atmosphere that comprise pollutants such as smoke, dust, and industrial emissions, which combine with water vapour. This massive scale of air pollution has occurred so frequently it is now referred to as the “haze season”.

But this year’s haze has been extremely serious. It has been going on for about 2 months and no indication of stopping, further exacerbated by the El Niño weather system, which has brought drier conditions to the region. It is still treated as a “natural disaster”, however, ordinary people are suffering the consequences of actions by large agriculture companies, proven by countless studies and activists on the field.

Oil palms are not native to Malaysia or Indonesia, yet these two countries are at the heart of Southeast Asia’s palm oil empire, accounting for roughly 85% of global palm oil production. European colonial powers first introduced oil palms to the region as ornamental plants. However, as rubber markets declined after World War I, colonial plantation economies began shifting towards oil palm as a new profitable commodity, transforming vast stretches of land in Malaya and Indonesia into plantations.

This shift came at a devastating cost. Native plants, traditional food systems and self-sufficient ways of life were disrupted or destroyed to make way for commercial agriculture. Indigenous communities and local populations were displaced and subjected to exploitative labour systems, including indentured and contract labour, under colonial plantation regimes in the region. What was once a landscape shaped by diverse ecosystems and local livelihoods was increasingly reorganised around extraction and profit.

Today, the colonisers have left, but the plundering and destruction continues - this time by modern capitalist forces, driven by agribusinesses across Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. Vast areas of biodiverse tropical rainforest in Malaysia and Indonesia have been cleared for palm oil plantations, contributing to severe biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and deforestation.

The fires and transboundary haze that plague the region are also linked to a complex web of corporate ownership, plantation concessions and business interests. Companies identified in reporting and investigations into plantation-related fires and land clearing include Malaysian firms and Indonesian plantation operators connected to Singapore-based business groups.

Examples include: PT Damai Agro Sejahtera — affiliated with Singapore-headquartered Bumitama Agri Ltd; and PT Arjuna Utama Sawit — identified as part of First Borneo Plantations, a plantation business with reported Singapore connections, and more.

The underlying pattern remains strikingly familiar: land and forests are treated as resources to be extracted for profit for the colonial powers back then and agribusinesses today, while indigenous communities, local livelihoods and the environment bear the consequences. When the profit is fully extracted, no compensation is given to the people, and barely any conservation efforts are made.

Such is the case with capitalism, where the world’s resources are exploited for the benefit of the few, while ordinary …

author: Ella Marchionda
title: Big opposition to WA government’s mega-university merger proposal
content:
The Western Australian Labor government is pushing ahead with its proposal to merge three of WA’s four public universities despite huge opposition among students, staff and the broader community. If the proposal to merge the University of Western Australia (UWA), Curtin University and Murdoch University goes ahead, the result will be a “mega-university” of 120,000 students, making it the biggest in the country. Both staff and students know that the merger will result in job losses, course reductions, larger class sizes and a decline in education quality. 

The proposed merger represents a corporate reorganisation of our universities to more effectively align with the priorities of capitalism in the state, particularly in defence and resources. Mark Barnaba, deputy chair of mining giant Fortescue Metals, will head the steering committee. 

The state government’s reasoning is straightforward: Western Australian universities are falling short in meeting industry needs, and their research income trails behind that of east coast universities. Nonetheless, the universities are already largely controlled by the needs of industry. Curtin University is already involved in the government’s “Critical Minerals Trailblazer programme,” which aims to “accelerate the commercialisation of university research” by increasing business investment in research and development related to defence and critical minerals. UWA hosts the Defence & Security Institute, which promotes the $368 billion AUKUS nuclear submarine program. 

The main problem with education is not that it isn't sufficiently competitive, but that it’s run as a business. Universities operate as degree factories, treating education as a commodity and students as consumers. University governance boards are more and more led by industry executives and those with corporate and business expertise, placing financial goals at the forefront. 

The corporate nature of universities has been highlighted by huge cost-cutting measures at multiple universities around the country, where staff, students and courses are attacked while executives’ million-dollar pay packages are protected.  Sydney’s UTS recently paid $7 million to KPMG to design course cuts and organisational restructures. Universities use faux crisis narratives to rationalize these cuts, with a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry reporting that six universities exaggerated financial issues to push through course and staff reductions.  In 2021, UWA implemented significant reductions in staff positions and the anthropology and sociology majors.  Murdoch University recently announced that budget cuts were necessary because of a decline in international student enrolments. A university system that relies on international students as cash cows is toxic.  

The proposed merger will only intensify corporate control of the university system. The new university will continue to have overpaid executives and rising student fees. The government-commissioned Deloitte report titled “Rapid Cost-Benefit Analysis” suggests that raising international student fees could increase revenue for the new university. But the recently merged Adelaide University has already revealed serious risks to university staff and the overall standard of education. Last month, the university introduced a voluntary early retirement scheme and indicated that voluntary redundancies might be considered. 

The proposed merger is extremely unpopular: two-thirds of National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) members polled on the plan are against it. On 21 October, 300 students and staff rallied outside state parliament to oppose the merger. The turnout was impressive at the semester's end when students are swamped with assignments.  Students expressed concerns about the potential loss of Indigenous Studies courses, while staff worry the change will result in larger classes and heavier workloads. 

Rojin Didari, a member of Socialist Alternative and one of the speakers, stated what must be made clear: 

“There is nothing good about this merger. It is not about the betterment of our education. It is not about staff and students.  It is about corporate interests.”

Liberal Party Shadow Education Minister Liam Staltari addressed the protest after being invited by Curtin Guild President Dylan Storer. author: José Soeiro, Maria Manuel Rola
title: A new cycle of struggle in Portugal
content:
At the end of last June, the left and the labour movement in Portugal secured an unlikely victory: the government’s proposed labour reform, which would have overhauled the Labour Code from top to bottom, was defeated in parliament.

Public pressure was so intense — with two general strikes, dozens of protests and a campaign that rallied the majority of public opinion against the government’s violently regressive agenda — that the far right, fearful of the electoral consequences of seeing its support for such a thoroughly unpopular proposal through to the end, changed its position and ultimately joined forces with the left to vote down the government’s labour reform package.

This struggle ushered in a new cycle of confidence for the popular movement.

The government, which holds a minority in parliament, put labour issues on hold and sought to change the subject. It ensured that the Socialist Party [PS] abstained on the draft state budget, on the one hand, and, on the other, reached an agreement with the far right on a new rental law which, in practice, virtually eliminates any rights for tenants.

A two-month delay in paying rent can lead to eviction. There is no longer a cap on deposits for renting a property. The number of months’ rent a tenant must pay in advance when signing a tenancy agreement has been increased to three. The 2% cap on rent increases has been removed.

With this proposal, the rental market — which is used by those unable to buy a home — becomes even more cut-throat, in the euro zone country where house prices have risen the most, where only 2% of housing is social housing, where the rent per square metre has doubled over the last five years, where, on average, people spend 50 per cent of their income on rent for legally registered tenancies alone (that is to say, it is even worse if we take the informal market into account), and where the poverty rate rises from around 15% to 27% when housing costs are factored in.

The rising cost of living, including fuel prices, and the approval (albeit without a final vote yet) of the tenancy law have created the conditions for a new cycle of protests.

A coalition of various groups and associations, called “Não Dá Mais” (“We Can’t Take It Anymore”), organised demonstrations against the rising cost of living in five cities, on October 10, attended by several thousand people. In Porto, which has the greatest impact in the north of the country, this demonstration coincided with two other protests — in support of Palestine and to safeguard an old market (the Bulhão), which is highly symbolic for the city — and was followed by a call, inspired by events in Spain and the wave of outrage over Maricarmen’s death, to set up a tent camp at the end of the rally, occupying the square where it had taken place.

On the first night, around 30 tents were pitched and remained in place. On the second night, there were more than 50. The camp was going to be cleared by the council at the end of the second night. The activists used social media to call for a new demonstration at the same location, with the aim of deciding, at an open-air public assembly, whether to resume the sit-in. On that same day, the Mayor declared that he would be “absolutely uncompromising” if the square were to be occupied with tents again. But not even that deterred the organisers of the camp, who set it up once more, with more people and more support.

At 3am, with no journalists left in the square, the government and the city council, acting in concert, ordered a brutal police charge against a few dozen peaceful activists who had spent the night in that square. Curiously, this was on the very same day that, 20 years ago, a movement had begun to occupy the municipal theatre located in the same square.

The mobile phone videos shocked public opinion and the city. That very same day, thousands of people flocked to the square in outrage, in a massive demonstration that also made its way to the entrance of the city hall. Not only did the movement explode, but it also began to spark reactions in other cities and a huge wave of solidarity.

Not even the attempts by the government and some commentators to stigmatise and blame the activists for having “provoked the police” had any effect.

For the past 10 days, the square has been constantly filled with thousands of people in the late afternoon and evening, with cultural events and workshops, whilst the organisers manage the day-to-day running of catering …

author: Lance Selfa
title: What to expect in the US midterm elections
content:
The Republican Party, also known as the GOP or Grand Old Party, controls both chambers of the US Congress, allowing President Donald Trump to pursue his far-right agenda with little legislative resistance. But that may soon change.

In the United States, federal elections occur every two years. The congressional midterms, so named because they occur in the middle of a president’s term, will be held on Tuesday. Polling suggests Republicans will be trounced. Voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, who serve fixed two-year terms, and about one-third of the 100 Senators, who serve six-year terms. A range of state-level races, including for governors in California, Michigan and Florida, will also take place.

The Democratic Party is expected to win back control of the House and possibly even the Senate. But just how much difference will that make?

Lance Selfa

, author of

The Democrats: A Critical History

 and editor of

US Politics in an Age of Uncertainty

, previews the elections and what might come after them.

Multiple indicators point to a Democratic victory in the midterm elections. Trump is an historically unpopular president. Gasoline and diesel prices are at their highest in years because of Trump’s war in Iran.

Consumer confidence is at a 73-year low

, and

74 percent of Americans

 tell pollsters that the country is moving in the wrong direction.

So it’s no surprise that Democrats are favoured to win the House. In fact, Republicans have given up trying to forestall that.

Data-driven forecasters like G. Elliott Morris

 and Nate Silver place the probability of a Democratic House higher than 90 percent, and the probability of the Democrats winning the Senate at 70 percent or higher.

The well-regarded

New York Times

 poll

, published 21 October, estimated that, were the election held then, Democrats would receive 52 percent of the vote, compared to 41 percent for the Republicans. If that holds, it will be the biggest Democrat popular-vote margin in a midterm election since the Watergate scandal brought down the Republicans in 1974.

That result wouldn’t represent an endorsement for the Democratic Party, which remains as unpopular as the Republicans. But US midterm elections are classically “throw the bums out” elections. And the Republicans, who control all parts of the national government, are the bums this year.

Trump and his toadies declare the polls “fake” and promise a Republican victory. But their behaviour—Trump, Vice President Vance and other administration figures are campaigning almost exclusively in “red” conservative areas—suggests they know they are in deep trouble. Polls currently show that the Senate race in Kansas, where Democrats haven’t won since 1932, is a toss-up. And Democrat James Talarico is slightly favoured to win a Senate seat in Texas, where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide since the 1990s.

The last-minute campaign blitz and the truly obscene amount of money billionaires are spending to shore up Republican candidates may limit GOP losses. It seems clear, however, that the Democrats are headed for victory next week. The real question will be how high the Democratic wave will crest.

What will Trump do?

All the above assumes that 3 November will unfold as a “normal” midterm election. But Trump and his minions are talking openly about challenging or overturning the results. Given Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, nothing is “off the table”.

Trump, his captive Supreme Court, and Republicans at all levels of government have conducted a years-long campaign to disenfranchise sections of the population and undermine democracy. This includes the Supreme Court’s evisceration of the Voting Rights Act, gerrymandering to lock in GOP majorities, and Trump’s so-far failed attempt to use the US Postal Service to make mail-in voting more difficult.

Trump and his Justice Department have continued to act on the lie that non-US citizens are voting illegally. The DOJ has tried to force state governments, constitutionally responsible for running US elections, to hand over their voter rolls. With voting data in hand, the Trump government says it can purge non-citizens from the rolls. So far, no state has complied, and the courts have ruled against Trump and the DOJ.

However, the DOJ has persisted. In late October, it indicted 28 individuals in California whom it claims voted illegally. Moreover, it sent lists of supposed non-citizen voters …

author: Ben Radford
title: UN General Assembly votes to end US blockade of Cuba — again
content:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-thirty countries voted in favour of the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba” on October 28, with 17 against and 25 abstentions.

Every year since 1992, the UNGA has overwhelmingly voted to end the blockade. However, this year, there was a rise in votes against and abstentions, likely reflective of new far-right governments — for example, in Colombia, Chile and Honduras — coming to power since last year’s vote. The US has also ramped up its international efforts to isolate Cuba through sanctions and threats of sanctions against countries that trade with Cuba.

This year’s vote took place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

The Cuban government submitted its annual report to the UNGA in September, detailing last year’s impacts of the US blockade. Between March last year and February this year, the blockade inflicted more than US$8 billion worth of damages.

The economic cost of just four days of the blockade amounts to the cost of all fuel imports needed to meet Cuba’s demand.

On top of existing strangulation mechanisms, the US government imposed an energy blockade on Cuba in January, claiming that the country posed an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to US national security.

The US announced tariffs on goods from countries that, directly or indirectly, sold or provided oil to Cuba. Following the US’s January 3 attacks on Venezuela, it also blocked all Venezuelan oil shipments to the country.

The energy blockade is the reason for widespread blackouts, as well as disruptions to water supply, waste collection and transport.

The fuel shortages are severely impacting hospital operations, including treatments that require a steady energy supply, such as haemodialysis. There are harrowing reports of surgeons having to perform operations by mobile phone lights, due to the blackouts.

The US blockade has affected Cubans’ access to vital treatment and medicine. One example is Cuba’s cancer survival rates, which, while still higher than many low- and middle-income countries, have dropped from 85% to 65%.

Cuba’s infant mortality has risen from 4 out of 1000 live births in 2018 to 9.9 last year — a 148% rise.

Cuban authorities say that the current transport crisis is more acute than during the “Special Period” in the 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union, which plunged Cuba into a prolonged economic crisis. Fuel shortages have affected refrigerated transport, preventing more than 30,000 children from receiving vaccines.

In May, the US imposed a regime of secondary sanctions against governments and companies that invest in or trade with Cuba.

For example, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control has imposed fines on US companies for handling cargo shipments bound for Cuba and providing services for people living in the country.

Over the past year, 34 international banking institutions suspended or declined to conduct operations with Cuba, citing risks of secondary sanctions.

Several airlines have ceased operations in Cuba and many international hotel chains also abandoned management agreements for hotels, citing the risks posed by the secondary sanctions regime. These sanctions — along with other US measures — have contributed to the collapse in Cuba’s tourism industry.

“The application of these measures has produced a sophisticated mechanism of asphyxiation directed at the Cuban population, exceeding by far the levels of pressure historically imposed over decades,” the annual report said.

It also notes that the blockade has caused US$3.9 trillion worth of damages since it was imposed. However, it said the impacts go far beyond economic losses, causing suffering, illness and death.

The US blockade of Cuba violates not just international law, but any semblance of humanity.

The US government has made its intention of achieving “regime change” in Cuba by the end of the year very clear; it is openly considering the possibility of military attacks. This has been the US’s policy since Cubans overthrew the …

author: Robert Narai
title: Days of hope and rage in France
content:
At the centre of Paris, the Monument à la République looms over a square that has hosted every great mobilisation of the French left in modern history. The bronze statue of Marianne, symbol of the Republic, holds an olive branch above the words: 

Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité.

 During mass demonstrations on 17 October, dozens of young people scaled the monument while tens of thousands looked on. Some flew Palestinian and red flags. On the statue of 

Egalité

, someone had scrawled “jeunesse dorée” (“gilded youth”, an old term for the idle rich). Marianne herself was draped in a giant yellow vest bearing the words: “The police mutilate high school students”.

For almost a month now, a mass student revolt has been rocking France, in one of the deepest political crises seen in the country in decades. The state that claims to embody liberty, equality and fraternity has answered 

lycéens

 (high schoolers aged 15 to 18) demanding better conditions in schools with tear gas, rubber bullets and mass arrests. That the Republic’s police are maiming young people in the streets is an indictment of the capitalist system the Republic protects.

Days of rage

In response to a national day of action on 17 October, in which an estimated 800,000 people protested across France, the government of Emmanuel Macron unleashed a flurry of violence.

Police fired tear gas into the crowd gathering at Place de la République before the march had formed. Riot police armed with batons, shields and armoured vehicles charged into crowds in Paris, Lyons, Bordeaux and a string of provincial cities, attacking protesters and bystanders alike. According to the Interior Ministry, almost 1,800 people were arrested and more than 500 police were injured, with 855 arrests in Paris alone. A teenager lost a hand in Saint-Étienne and another lost an eye in Mulhouse. Street medics were dragged along the ground by police.

The new element on 17 October was the return of the Yellow Vests, the leaderless movement of rural and provincial workers against fuel taxes and the high cost of living that erupted in 2018, until it was crushed with brute force by the state. After weeks of watching 

lycéens

 face down riot police, the Yellow Vests called their own day of action protesting the cost of living. The Yellow Vests blocked roundabouts and fuel depots from the morning and declared their support for the student revolt. Among them was Pierre, a retiree from Bandol: “I’ve been gassed five times since this morning”, he told 

La Provence

. “[Macron’s government] is declaring war on the people.” The return of the Yellow Vests raises the possibility of the student revolt becoming a rallying point for broader working-class grievances.

Nurses, teachers and firefighters joined the Yellow Vests demonstration. In Lille, 20 rail workers marched together in their SNCF vests. Most of the working class support the movement (55 percent of the French population support the student-led protest movement, according to an Elabe poll) but are not yet part of it.

Whose Republic?

The Macron government’s strategy has been to paint the victims of violence as its perpetrators. Prime Minister Lecornu blamed “far-left groups”, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez targeted “ultra-left individuals”, while Macron declared that “nothing can explain, nothing can excuse” the violence. They pointed to a handful of burnt buildings, such as the town hall in Limoges, to paint a movement of hundreds of thousands as a mindless mob. “The perpetrators directly targeted the institutions of the Republic and the authority of the State”, wrote Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave.

It is worth asking what sort of Republic the mayor of Bordeaux is defending: one in which a burnt town hall causes enormous outrage, but a sixteen-year-old losing an eye to a police grenade prompts hysteria about the need for more law and order.

The ruling class never calls the conditions that produced this revolt violence. Students in France’s poorest schools sit in classrooms infested with cockroaches and rats, in classes of up to 35. Outside school, the police stop, search and arrest young Black and Arab men from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) for the colour of their skin and the estate they live on, and their operations now cause more than one death per week. Fuel and food prices keep rising, while, according to Oxfam, 53 billionaires own as much as the poorest 48 percent of the population. This is the systematic violence …
